* fix(vscode,docs): gitignore .env in scaffolded projects (#1201)

Connecting to a self-hosted engine writes a real ROCKETRIDE_APIKEY into
the workspace .env (Connection.syncEnvFile), but ensureGitignore only ever
added `.rocketride/`. A fresh project was one `git add .` away from
committing a live key.

- ensureGitignore now reconciles a list of entries (`.rocketride/`, `.env`)
  and appends only the missing ones, so it never duplicates a line.
- The pure reconciliation moves to shared/util/gitignoreEntries.ts, which
  is vscode-free and therefore unit-testable -- the same seam envFile.ts
  already uses. Matching is on exact trimmed lines: a user who wrote
  `*.env` keeps their own rule and gets a redundant line at worst, which
  beats us second-guessing their config.
- Agent checklist: adds an explicit "make sure .env is gitignored" step,
  renames `env.example` -> `.env.example` (also in COMPONENT_REFERENCE),
  and replaces "open .env as a visible tab" with verifying the variable
  names the pipeline actually expects.

Note `.env` does not match `.env.example`, so the example file stays
committable -- covered by a test.

Verified: 8/8 node:test pass; tsc --noEmit clean; prettier clean.

* docs: point every docs.rocketride.ai reference at .org (#1534)

The issue names .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/config.yml, but two more remained:
.github/SUPPORT.md and the rocketride package docstring in
packages/client-python/src/rocketride/__init__.py -- the last of which
ships to PyPI and is the most user-visible of the three.

`grep -rn docs.rocketride.ai` is now empty.

* fix(vscode): preserve .gitignore trailing content when appending (#1737 review)

appendGitignoreEntries trimmed the content before appending, which dropped
any blank lines the user left at the end of their .gitignore. It also
emitted a leading newline for whitespace-only content, because the
separator was decided from the untrimmed string while the prefix used the
trimmed one.

Now the existing text is preserved byte-for-byte and a separator is added
only when it does not already end in a newline. A hand-edited .gitignore
is the user's file; reformatting it while adding one line is how a tool
loses trust.

Two regression tests added for the whitespace-only and trailing-blank-line
cases. 10/10 node:test pass.

* fix(ai): verify a task port can be bound before handing it out

`assign_port` picked the first number it had not issued yet and never asked
the OS whether the port was usable. A port inside a Windows exclusion range,
one held by a concurrently running engine, or one just released while its
previous owner still held the socket was handed out anyway; the child failed
to bind and the parent surfaced a bare "connection refused".

- probe the candidate with a real `bind` and move on when it fails
- tell `EACCES` from `EADDRINUSE`: cache only the former, since a busy port's
  owner can exit at any moment
- name the cause when a window is exhausted, and point the reader inward when
  the ports are held by this server rather than by anything external
- wait for uvicorn's bound listener instead of its lifespan hook, which fires
  before the socket exists, and stop routing debugpy's bind failure into the
  stdlib logger where it vanished

* fix(ai): address review on the port-bind probe

- take a set snapshot of `_allocated_ports` for the membership test; the
  list stays the source of truth for `release_port`, but a linear scan per
  candidate made a full window quadratic on the path that blocks the loop
- say "most of the range" / "most probes failed", since the named cause is
  the plurality and the tallies printed beside it were contradicting the
  absolute wording
- check the serve() future while waiting for the startup callback, so a
  failure that precedes the callback surfaces at once rather than at the
  deadline; the existing blocking wait is kept, sliced

The blocking-wait test stubbed its future with a bare mock whose `done()`
is truthy, which would have ended the wait immediately once it consults
the future; the stub now reports pending, as a live `serve()` does.

* fix(ai): address review on the port-bind probe

Blocking:

- report a failed `debugpy.listen` through engLib `warning`, not `debug`.
  `debug()` returns early unless the DebugOut level is enabled, so the
  previous change had made that failure quieter than the stdlib logger it
  replaced, not louder
- drop cached OS reservations and re-probe once before declaring a window
  exhausted. Windows exclusion ranges are released as Hyper-V, WSL and
  Docker stop, so the usable window could otherwise only ever shrink
- stop a bare `MagicMock` future from short-circuiting the timeout test,
  which left the deadline break with no coverage at all

Also:

- an fd ceiling no longer becomes a launch refusal: when every probe failed
  for reasons of ours rather than the pool's, hand back an unverified port
  as the old allocator did
- name a tied cause, and say when the window was clamped below 10000
- diagnose a `serve()` future that completes cleanly before the listener
  appears — the one path that returned a silently dead server
- snapshot `_allocated_ports` into a set for membership, bound the listener
  poll by the shared deadline, and check the future while waiting for the
  startup callback

  diagnostics, so the sidebar chips honor the documented contract —
  chips describe the LAST run until the next begin/restart resets them.

* fix(nodes): filestore source — empty-path guard, source-parameters shape, engine render contract

Fixes the three defects found by the File Store Source live smoke test:

- D1: scanObjects now raises 'File Store Source: "path" is required' when the
  resolved path param is empty/blank, instead of silently enumerating and
  pushing the user's entire account store root.
- D3: services.source.json routes filesystem.path/filesystem.recursive through

  declared fields actually reach the endpoint as serviceConfig['parameters']
  (engine strips the field prefix; form emits config.parameters).
- D2: delivery moved from the telegram-style target-pipe push to the engine's
  DIRECT pipeline contract (Pipeline.cpp: "Connect the scanObjects function to
  the renderObject function"): scanObjects reports each file through the scan
  callback (feeding the scanner's object counter), and IInstance.renderObject
  delegates to IEndpoint.renderStoreObject which sends the bytes as a raw tag
  stream via sendTag* + preventDefault. Successful runs no longer end with the
  spurious "Files not found" warning, and totals/completed/failed accounting
  now comes from the engine (verified live: 2/2, 3/3, 1/1; exactly one object
  per file downstream; task subprocess exits 0).

Note: task status still shows exitCode 1 for every task because of a
pre-existing harness key mismatch (transport_stdio emits apaevt_exit body key
'exitCode', task_engine reads 'exit_code' and defaults to 1) — out of scope
here, tracked as a follow-up in packages/ai.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(ai): auto-provision ephemeral RR_SIGNING_KEY at web-server startup

Local (filesystem-backend) deployments needed a manually configured
RR_SIGNING_KEY before FileStore.get_url / emitUrl signed links worked.
Generate a random key at startup when the operator set none — same
self-provisioning channel RR_BASE_URL already uses; task subprocesses
inherit it. Cloud backends presign natively and never read it. Signed
URLs stop verifying after a restart, acceptable at the 1-hour TTL cap.

Also stub rocketlib in the web-server test harness so the suite runs
outside the builder environment.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(nodes): pin File Store media streams to one persistent event loop

aiofiles write handles bind to the loop that opened them; the sink's
_run_async spins a fresh asyncio.run loop per lane callback, so the
first chunk after open_write hit 'Event loop is closed' and every
streamed image/audio/video aborted as a 0-byte file. Handle-based ops
(open_write/write_chunk/close_write and the abort path) now run on a
dedicated long-lived loop thread; one-shot ops keep per-call loops.

Found live via the sink UI test; the engine masked the real error with
a garbage UnicodeDecodeError from a dangling string_view in the

* fix(nodes): File Store Source closes each object explicitly

The dev-mode runner, unlike task-mode processItem, never closes the

* fix(nodes): register engine render thread with pydevd before traced code runs

Designer dev-mode tasks run under debugpy; renderObject executes on the

…generic SaveFileDialog (browser) (#1902)

* feat(save-dialog): native untitled pipeline flow (VS Code) + revived generic SaveFileDialog (browser)

VS Code — pipeline creation and save now follow the standard document
lifecycle instead of a save-dialog-first flow that wrote a file up front:

- "New pipeline" (sidebar) and a new File > New File... entry both mint a
  NAMELESS, path-less untitled .pipe and open it in the grid editor. A
  path-bearing untitled URI silent-saves (and errors "file already exists"),
  so the document deliberately carries no path — first save runs a dialog.
- Ctrl+S (keybinding scoped to the grid editor) and the webview Save button
  share one flow (savePipeline.ts / pipelineSave.ts): titled files save in
  place; untitled ones open the native OS Save dialog defaulted INTO the
  configured pipelines directory (created first so it can't fall back to the
  process CWD — the demo bug) with a .pipe filter. Native untitled Save As
  can target neither a subfolder nor force the extension, hence the driven
  dialog. On confirm the file is written, the untitled buffer is
  reverted-and-closed, and the saved .pipe reopens in the grid editor.
- Untitled content is auto-backed-up to workspaceState on every edit and
  restored on reopen, because VS Code hot-exit does not preserve a
  custom-editor untitled document across a restart — without this, unsaved
  nodes were lost and the canvas came back blank. The backup is cleared when
  the editor closes (save or discard), so only a full exit restores it. An
  empty restored untitled re-seeds the empty-pipeline template so it shows
  the starting-point wizard, never a blank canvas.

Save button now shows its brand-highlighted "savable" state for new/untitled
pipelines (isNew), not only when dirty, so an untitled pipeline correctly
indicates it can be saved (title becomes "Save As...").

Browser — revived the generic, VFS-backed shell SaveFileDialog (multiple
file types via a "Save as type" dropdown) and wired rocket-ui's pipeline
save to it through a new projectVfs adapter; removed the old rocket-ui
SaveDialog and usePipelineTree. Fixes: the name input collapsed to zero
width (it inherited inputField's width:100% via the extension suffix, hiding
typed text) and now grows correctly; a typed extension is no longer doubled
and dotted names are allowed; typing a known type's extension auto-selects
that type. api.ts changes are export-only additions (SaveFileDialog + its
types) — the frozen v0 contract and contract-check are untouched.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(save-dialog): address CodeRabbit review — run gating, path containment, dialog robustness

Nine findings from the #1902 review, why each matters:

- vscode run flow: an untitled pipeline could RUN unsaved — the
  status:pipelineAction handler's saveDocument() sees identical content and
  no-ops, never naming the buffer. savePipelineDocument now returns the saved
  target URI (undefined on cancel/no-workspace/failed save) and the run
  handler drives the full untitled save flow first, running only from a
  successful save; a cancelled Save dialog cancels the run. Text is captured
  before the save because the untitled buffer is closed by it.
- pipelineSave: rocketride.defaultPipelinePath is contractually
  workspace-relative, but absolute paths, drive-qualified paths, and ..
  segments escaped the workspace and got mkdir'd. Escaping values now fall
  back to the documented 'pipelines' default.
- projectVfs: read/write/rename/delete/mkdir were plain arrows, so a
  requireClient() failure threw synchronously — contradicting the
  IVirtualFileSystem Promise contract and escaping .catch() handlers. All
  members are now async and reject.
- rocket-ui save-as: the dialog opened at root with an empty name; it now
  preselects the document's folder (defaultDir) and name (initialName).
- SaveFileDialog:
  - listRecursive fans out sibling directories via Promise.all — each list
    is a server round trip, so the sequential walk held "Loading folders..."
    for the sum of every directory's latency.
  - extension matching is now case-insensitive everywhere (context-file
    filter, hasChildren, and the overwrite-confirm set) so "flow.PIPE" is
    shown and can no longer be silently overwritten on a case-insensitive
    store.
  - keyboard users can now expand folders: ArrowRight/ArrowLeft on the row,
    and the chevron is a focusable button with aria-expanded.
  - activeType falls back to an extension-less type when a host passes an
    empty fileTypes array (public shell API; previously a TypeError).
  - a saving flag blocks confirm re-entry, so double Enter/Save during the

* feat(nodes): add tool_gohighlevel CRM tool node

Exposes the GoHighLevel (LeadConnector) v2 REST API to agents as 101 tools
across 17 resource groups, plus a generic request tool that reaches any
remaining v2 endpoint through the same auth, rate-limit and read-only layer.

Authentication is a sub-account Private Integration Token only. OAuth is
deliberately absent: GoHighLevel refresh tokens are single-use and rotating,
and a node has nowhere durable to persist the replacement, so an OAuth
credential would work for 24h, refresh, discard the new token, and die
unrecoverably a day later with no config-only recovery.

Full coverage is more tools than an LLM chooses between reliably, so
gohighlevel.toolGroups controls which groups publish; the default ten groups
publish 74 tools. Read-only mode hides every write tool rather than only
refusing it at invoke time, so a read-only agent never sees a tool it cannot
use.

Client details specific to GoHighLevel, each verified against a live
sub-account rather than the published docs:

- Version is a per-operation header, not a global constant: 2021-04-15 for
  calendars and conversations, 2021-07-28 elsewhere.
- There is no response envelope. Every endpoint names its own top-level key,
  and the key is not always the resource, so call() does not unwrap and each
  tool names its key.
- GET /opportunities/search requires location_id in snake case and rejects
  the camelCase form with a 422; every other endpoint is camelCase.
- Retry on 429 only. A 403 means a missing locationId or agency-scope
  refusal, so retrying it burns budget and hides the real error.
- Rate-limit budgets are read from response headers, never assumed: a trial
  token measured 25 requests per 10s and 10,000 per day, against the 100 per
  10s and 200,000 per day published for marketplace apps.
- x-ratelimit-daily-reset is a duration in milliseconds, not an epoch.
- Ids are opaque 20 to 24 character strings, so id validation is string-based.

Tests: 203 unit tests that need no credentials or network, plus an env-gated
live suite behind GHL_PIT and GHL_LOCATION_ID, with record-creating tests
additionally behind GHL_ALLOW_WRITES.

* feat(nodes): let the File Store sink choose what to do when a file exists

The sink always wrote under a fresh `_1`, `_2` name when the target was taken,
with no way to say otherwise. Re-running a pipeline into the same directory
therefore accumulated copies rather than replacing what was there.

Adds a `When the file already exists` setting with the three outcomes that
decision has: `unique` (the previous behaviour, still the default), `overwrite`
and `skip`.

Resolved once at config time into an `IntEnum` nested in `IGlobal`, so each write
compares ints; member names are the services.store.json enum values, which is what
resolves one to the other. Anything that does not name a member falls back to
`unique`, so a mistyped config degrades to the non-destructive outcome rather than
failing the pipeline.

`skip` makes `_sink_target_path` return None, which callers must read as "leave it
alone" rather than as an error: no file is written and no reference is emitted for it.

* fix(nodes): don't delete a file the sink did not create

Review follow-up.

- Cleanup after an interrupted stream now removes only a file this stream created.
  Under unique/skip the path was probed free, so the partial output is ours; under
  overwrite it is the operator's existing file and deleting it turned a transient
  failure into permanent loss
- skip compares against an existing file, not any entry, so a directory sharing the
  name no longer drops the output
- OnConflict moved to module level: IInstance imports it directly and the test stubs
  no longer patch it onto a shared class
- The skip warning is emitted from _sink_target_path alone

The stat mock returned only `exists`, and the read-size-cap stub did not export
OnConflict; both now match the surfaces they stand in for.

* fix(nodes): stage an overwrite and swap it in only when it is complete

Not deleting the destination on failure was not enough: opening it is already
destructive. Verified against a real FileStore — `open_write` truncates the file
to 0 bytes before a single byte is written, so an interrupted stream left the
operator's data neither old nor new.

Under overwrite the stream now writes to a sibling `<path>.part-<objectId>` and
renames over the destination once the file is complete. The destination is not
opened at all until then, so a failure anywhere leaves it untouched, and the
cleanup is unambiguous: the staging file is always ours to delete.

- unique/skip are unchanged; their path was probed free, so there is nothing to
  protect and no rename to pay for
- the staging path is whitelist-checked like any other. A whitelist that admits
  the destination but not a sibling falls back to writing in place with a
  warning, rather than failing a pipeline that worked before
- this also settles the deferred-commit half of the review: the destination is
  never staged over, so no abort path on FileStore is needed after all

* fix(ai): move files natively instead of reading them through memory

Adds move_file to the store interface and implements it per backend: os.replace
on a filesystem, CopyObject on S3, start_copy_from_url on Azure. Each leaves the
destination untouched until the new content is in place, and none of them pull
the bytes through this process.

FileStore.rename now uses it. It previously read the whole file into memory and
wrote it over the destination, so replacing a large file spiked memory by its
size and a failure part-way left the destination damaged.

Also fixes the branch it took to get there: a plain file was treated as a
directory, because listing a path's prefix returns the file sitting at that path
and rename counted it as a child. stat() already excluded it; rename now does
the same. Measured on a real store: renaming a 64 MB file moved peak memory
from 64 MB to 0.

* fix(nodes): discard the stream when a chunk write fails

Review follow-up (CodeRabbit).

An exception from write_chunk left the stream in place: the handle stayed open,
holding the store's write lock, and the partial file sat there until the next
object's open() swept it. It is now discarded and the error re-raised.

Also excludes filesystem.onConflict from the tool variant's contract test, so a
future service merge cannot expose sink configuration on tool_filesystem://
without failing it.

* fix(nodes): report a cleanup that could not remove its staging file

Found by driving the sink against a real store with the store broken on purpose:
when close_write fails without releasing the OS handle, the delete that follows
fails too, and the staging file stays in the target directory. The destination
was safe in every case, but the leftover was silent — the path is now named in a
warning rather than swallowed.

Also drops a comment that staging had made wrong: it said replacing needs no
truncate because open_write opens 'wb'. That still holds for a one-shot write,
but a streamed overwrite no longer opens the destination at all. Trims three
others that had grown past the point they were making.

* fix(nodes,ai): CodeRabbit review on the File Store sink

- `rename` refuses a path that is both a file and a directory
- Azure's server-side copy passes `requires_sync` and checks the status
- tests assert cleanup order (close before delete) and the staging path

Also trims comments and docstrings, and corrects the README: with staging
in place, an interrupted `overwrite` leaves the existing file untouched.

…s stay valid (#1915)

* fix(server): intern Python caller location names so ap::Location views stay valid

`getPythonCallerLocation()` returned owning `std::string`s, but `ap::Location`
stores `std::string_view` and `Error` keeps the location by value. The `Error`
handed to the monitor outlived the tuple its views pointed into, so later reads
of the location — `completionError` among them — touched freed memory.

- Intern file and function names in a process-lifetime pool and hand out views
  into it
- Return `string_view` from the helper, making the lifetime explicit at the call
  site

The pool is an `unordered_set`, which is node-based, so an insert never moves a
string another view already points at. It is never pruned — that is what keeps
the views valid for the life of the process — and a pipeline's distinct
file/function names are bounded by its Python sources, so it stays small.

* fix(server): leak the caller-location intern pool so it outlives the monitor

`internPool` and `internLock` were ordinary function-local statics, so they were
destroyed at exit. `engine::config::monitor()` is a function-local static too and
is constructed at engine start, which makes it the last one destroyed - the pool
would already be gone while the monitor still held `Error`s viewing into it,
putting the same dangling read back at shutdown.

Allocate both with `new` and never delete them, so "life of the process" is
exact. The lock is leaked for the same reason as the pool: locking a destroyed
mutex from another thread during shutdown has the same shape of defect.

* feat(nodes): add db_hotdata, an ephemeral per-run database node

Wraps Hotdata (hotdata.dev) as a ["database","tool"] node giving a pipeline run
a disposable OLAP database: created lazily on first use, loaded with
NDJSON/CSV/Parquet, indexed, queried, then destroyed in endGlobal.

Fills the one structural gap in the catalogue - every other SQL, vector and
graph node writes to a persistent store, so an agent that wants to load a file,
index it and throw it away had only tool_python (no network) or the tenant's
production database.

Patterns matched, from a survey of the 11 database/graph-classed services:
- capabilities ["noremote","invoke"], unanimous across those nodes. noremote is
  load-bearing here: it clears PROTOCOL_CAPS::REMOTING, without which
  distributed instances would each create their own billed database.
- lanes {"answers": [], "questions": [...]}, matching the four ingest-and-query
  nodes; invoke.llm.min = 1 like every NL-querying database node.
- No DatabaseGlobalBase (SQLAlchemy, and Hotdata ships no dialect) - the
  graph_arango custom-client pattern instead.
- Lock-guarded lazy creation and endGlobal teardown copied from tool_daytona.

No new dependency pins: requests/urllib3/httpx are already baseline and
requests is already in constraints.lock, so the engine-wide solve cannot break.
The vendor SDK is deliberately unused.

Tests: 85 node unit tests (no network), 338 contract tests across the whole
catalogue, 12/12 live checks against a real Hotdata workspace, plus agentic and
SDK pipeline runs against a live engine.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(nodes): address CodeRabbit review findings on db_hotdata

Six issues from the review, each verified against current code first.

Retry-After: 0 is a legal header value that passed the `< 0` check and produced
a zero-length sleep, so a single 429 carrying it spun the retry loop with no
pause until the whole budget was spent - against a server that is already
shedding load. Floor the effective delay at BASE_BACKOFF_S.

The append dedup fingerprints describe one specific database, but
drop_database left them in place. After a drop the next get_database creates an
empty database, and an identical append then reported deduplicated without
loading. Clear them with the handle.

_await_job compared the 202 envelope status without lowercasing, while the
polled status was already lowercased. A 'Pending' envelope was treated as a
finished job, so load_data kept its dedup reservation for rows that never
landed and build_index reported a not-yet-built index as ready.

A partially_succeeded job returned normally, so load_data kept the reservation
even though only some rows landed and a retry would be skipped as a duplicate.
The partial state is now returned to the caller, which releases the reservation
and surfaces `partial` on the tool result.

writeAnswers caught every exception and only logged it. The answers lane has no
output lane to emit to, so the run reported success while the rows were never
loaded. It re-raises now; the client already retries transient failures.

execute duplicated the row-limit clamp instead of calling _resolve_limit, so
the two paths could diverge.

Job statuses checked against the published spec: JobStatus is
pending|running|succeeded|partially_succeeded|failed, which confirms the
_JOB_PENDING set.

Tests: 89 node unit tests (four new, one rewritten for the writeAnswers change),
338 contract tests, and 12/12 live checks against a real Hotdata workspace.

  `type` or `data_type` and `name` or `column_name`. A payload using the other

- _rows_to_markdown escaped pipes but not newlines, so any cell containing one

- The NL-to-SQL examples hardcoded LIMIT 250 while the instruction told the

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(nodes): correct partial-append handling in db_hotdata

Two follow-up findings from CodeRabbit's re-review, both against fixes made in
the previous commit.

Releasing the dedup reservation after a partially succeeded append was wrong.
Append is not idempotent - that is the whole reason the reservation exists - so
a partial load means an unknown subset of the payload already landed, and
letting a retry through duplicates exactly those rows. The previous change
traded silent data loss for silent duplication. A partial append now keeps its
reservation, and the note tells the caller what actually happened: query the
table and load only what is missing, because a blind retry will duplicate.
There is no safe automatic action for a partial non-idempotent load.

row_count fell back to len(rows) unconditionally, so a result_id load with no
server-reported count returned 0 - claiming an empty load that may well have
inserted rows. The fallback now applies only when inline rows were uploaded;
otherwise the count stays None, which is honest about being unknown.

The SHOW TABLES contradiction between hotdata_schema.py and hotdata_client.py
is resolved in favour of the live-verified behaviour: SHOW TABLES works, and
the DESCRIBE / SHOW COLUMNS gap is about a table having no data yet rather than
unsupported syntax. REST introspection is preferred for reliability, not as a
workaround.

schema, table and index names arrive as agent tool arguments and were

the fix: a table named '../../other' produced

endpoint, and 'orders?x=1' injected a query string. An agent - or a prompt
injection reaching one - could redirect the node's calls.

Identifiers are now refused rather than escaped: letters, digits, underscore,
dollar and hyphen only, up to 128 characters, checked at the client where the
interpolation happens so every call site is covered. This is the SSRF
containment the PR description already claimed and the acceptance criteria
already listed; it was never actually implemented.

row_count is omitted when the count is unknown rather than reported as null,
since the declared output schema defines it as an integer. A result_id load for
which Hotdata reports no count now simply has no row_count key.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(nodes): keep partial-append outcome across dedup in db_hotdata

The append reservation recorded only that a payload had been seen, not how it
finished. A partial append kept its fingerprint - correct, since append is not
idempotent and a blind retry duplicates whatever landed - but a later identical
call then fell into the dedup branch and returned the clean note claiming the
table already contains these rows. That contradicts the partial result, where
an unknown subset is missing.

The reservation now carries an outcome: pending while in flight, then complete
or partial. A repeat of a partial payload is still not re-sent, but reports
partial: true with the reconciliation instruction instead of the clean
duplicate note. record_load() sets the outcome once the job settles;
release_load() still clears the reservation when the load fails outright so a
genuine retry can run.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(nodes): distinguish pending from completed dedup in db_hotdata

seen_load() returns 'pending' while a load is still in flight, but the dedup
branch treated any prior reservation as a completed load. A concurrent caller
with the same payload was told the table already contains these rows before the
original load had finished - and if that original then failed and released the
reservation, the rows never landed at all.

The three reservation states are now distinct:

- pending  -> in_progress: true, no deduplicated flag and no row_count. The
              call makes no claim about the rows being present and tells the
              caller to wait for the in-flight load.
- partial  -> partial: true, and no row_count. The landed subset is unknown, so
              reporting the full input size overstated what is in the table.
- complete -> deduplicated: true with row_count, which is the only case where
              every row is known to have landed.

Regressions added for a concurrent in-flight duplicate and for
pending-then-failure, plus a row_count assertion on the repeated-partial case.
The concurrency test was verified to fail when the guard is disabled, so it is
not passing vacuously.

* feat(rocketlib): settle media streams in the shared node base (#1941)

A media lane carries no stream identifier, so a consumer keeps one slot of state
per lane and reads a fresh `BEGIN` as proof the previous stream ended. When one
object emits several streams on a lane that fails: the next `BEGIN` arrives while
the previous stream's `END` is still outstanding, every byte already delivered,
and the consumer discards a complete stream. Nothing was logged and the task
reported success.

`IInstanceBase` now normalizes this for every consumer at once. It counts the
bytes a stream receives, compares them against the size its own `BEGIN` declared,
and delivers the `END` the producer never sent. A handler therefore sees one
`BEGIN`, zero or more `WRITE`s and at most one `END` per stream, and needs no
bookkeeping of its own. A stream that fell short, carried no bytes, or declared
nothing is still dropped — now with a `warning` naming the object that lost it.

Wrapping happens in `__init_subclass__` rather than through a mixin or an opt-in
hook: a node that merely defines `writeImage()` would silently miss any scheme it
had to remember to join, and that silence is the failure being removed.

Also adds `audio_begin_payload` / `video_begin_payload` and the matching
`forward_enriched_*` helpers, so audio and video producers can declare their
stream size the way image producers already do.

* fix(tool_filesystem): sweep a cut-off media stream at closing() (#1942)

The File Store sink lost complete media streams when one object produced several:
the bytes arrived, were written, and were then removed again, with no warning and
a successful task. The settle that fixes that now lives in `IInstanceBase` (#1941),
which delivers the `END` a producer never sent — so this node needs no byte
accounting of its own and keeps only the half no shared base can do: releasing an
open write handle and the file behind it.

`open()` already dropped a stream the previous object left unfinished, but the last
object of a run gets no following `open()`. Without a sweep its partial file stayed
in the store for good — truncated under `unique`/`skip`, an orphaned `.part-*` under
`overwrite`. Adds `closing()` for that, with three tests covering it.

Also gives the commit path a name: the `END` branch's body moves into
`_media_commit` unchanged, so both a real `END` and the one the base synthesizes
take an identifiable route.

* fix(response): return nothing for an empty media stream (#1943)

The response node returned fewer media entries than the pipeline produced when one
object fanned out into several streams; the missing ones had been fully buffered
before being dropped. The settle that fixes that now lives in `IInstanceBase`
(#1941), which delivers each stream's `END` before the next `BEGIN` — so every
stream reaches the append path in turn and this node needs no bookkeeping of its
own.

`END` now returns early when the lane buffer is empty. Such a stream used to
produce an entry whose payload was an empty string; the File Store sink creates no
file for one either, so returning nothing is the consistent answer.

Adds the fan-out matrix to `test_media_metadata.py` — several streams on one lane,
a late `END`, a truncated stream, zero-length streams and three in a row — and
names the append path `_emit_media`.

* fix(frame_grabber): keep each video stream's own frame bookkeeping (#1963)

One object can carry several video streams, and a single `VideoFrameExtractor`
serves them in turn: the shared node base stops the reader at the end of one
stream and starts it again for the next. Two things leaked across that boundary.

`start()` reset the buffer and the done flag but never drained
`_frame_info_queue`. `onInfo` pushes `(frame_number, pts_time)` from the stderr
thread independently of PNG extraction, so a stream ending with entries still
unread handed its frame numbers and timestamps to the next one. It is drained
now.

`_processBuffer` waited on that queue with no timeout. It runs on the data
thread, so the opposite imbalance — a complete frame whose showinfo entry never
arrives — blocked that thread for good and left `stop()` hanging on its join.
The wait is bounded; on expiry the frame stays buffered for a later chunk and the
reason is logged.

In the node, `chunkId` and the per-frame name came from the frame's position in
its own video, and every video starts at zero. Two videos in one object produced
the same chunk ids and, since both streams share a parent and therefore a derived
stem, the same names. Both now come from the frame's ordinal within the object,
and the true position moves to `metadata.frame_number`. The image lane is named
the same way, so the two lanes agree on what a frame is called.

Reachable only after #1941: until the base settled media streams, a second BEGIN
raised `RuntimeError: FrameGrabber is already started` and the run failed loudly.
With the restart working, that became a silently wrong result.

* fix(thumbnail): number each thumbnail within its object (#1964)

One object can deliver several image streams — a cropper's crops, a frame
grabber's frames — and each thumbnail is its own chunk of that object. `chunkId`
was set to zero in `open()` and never advanced, so every document claimed chunk
0 and a consumer keyed on `(objectId, chunkId)` kept overwriting a single row: a
scan of three photographs produced three thumbnails and one record.

The counter now advances per emitted document. It stays inside the documents
branch because it labels documents only — the image lane takes its name from the
source descriptor, which already identifies the frame.

Reachable only after #1941: until the base settled media streams, a second BEGIN
displaced the first and just one stream ever reached the END handler, so one
chunk id was enough. `embedding_image` and `face_detection` already count this
way.

* fix(embedding_video): name frames by their ordinal in the object (#1965)

One object can carry several videos, and each video's frame positions start at
zero. The per-frame name used that position, so two videos in one object both
produced `<stem>.frame0`, `.frame30`, … — and since streams of one object share
a parent, the derived stem matched too, leaving nothing to tell the two sets
apart.

`chunkId` was already correct: `_frame_chunk_id` counts the object's frames and
does not restart between videos. Only the name disagreed with it. The name now
takes the same ordinal, so both labels point at one frame. The true position in
the video stays in `metadata.frame_number`.

Reachable only after #1941: until the base settled media streams, a second BEGIN
wiped the first video's buffer before it was ever decoded, so one object yielded
one video's frames and nothing could collide.

* fix(nodes): address review of the media-stream normalization

Scope the END contract to what the base actually guarantees. It supplies an END
only for a stream that received every byte its BEGIN declared; a producer's own
END is forwarded unread. Saying an END means the stream is complete promised a
check that does not happen, and contradicted the paragraph below it, which had
the undeclared single-stream case right.

`embedding_video` numbered frames from a counter that lived for the whole
instance. Instances are pooled and outlive an object, so the second object
opened wherever the first left off — and on which value depended on the instance
it was handed. Naming frames by that counter (#1965) carried the same
non-determinism into `metadata.name`, which was stable before. It resets per
object now.

`frame_grabber`'s table lane kept the per-video frame position while the other
two lanes moved to the ordinal (#1963). One table covers the whole object, so
several videos each contributed a row 0 and a row 1 with nothing to separate
them — and the table is the one output read directly.

A pending stream held back because its object failed was reported as one that
could not be settled. Every byte had arrived; the reason was the failure. The
report names it, and every path now marks the lane closed, so one lost stream
means one line rather than two.

`tool_filesystem` sweeps in-flight streams from one helper instead of two copies
of the same loop.

READMEs for the three nodes follow the output contracts that changed.

* docs(rocketlib): say what the media contract actually guarantees

Three overstatements in the wording added by the previous commit, one naming
slip.

The ended-or-reported guarantee skipped its own exception: a stream that neither
promised bytes nor delivered any is dropped without an END and without a line in
the log, because it lost nothing. Silence there is deliberate — a warning firing
on ordinary traffic is one nobody reads — but the sentence read as absolute.

An undeclared stream was described as lost whenever an object emits more than one
on a lane. Several of them in a row complete fine, each on its producer's own END.
Only the one whose END never comes is displaced by the next BEGIN, and that is the
missing END, not the count.

`frame_grabber`'s README defined `N` in `<video-stem>.frame<N>.png` as the frame
index in two places and only one was updated.

`embedding_video.open()` takes `obj`, matching `IInstanceBase` and leaving the
builtin alone.

* test(thumbnail): drive END with the buffer the engine sends

The helper called END with two arguments and relied on the media wrapper's default
to supply the third. It never failed — the wrapper's signature carries `buffer=b''`
— but the engine always passes a buffer on BEGIN and END, so the test was driving
the node in a shape it never sees.

* feat(llm): capture exact provider token usage in the Adapter for per-user billing

Read provider-reported usage (input/output tokens) at the normalized Adapter
(#1683) and report it via metrics.counter so per-user token accounting flows
through task_metrics/billing. One capture point covers all LangChain providers;
the native Anthropic extended-thinking and OpenAI Responses paths are
instrumented too.

* feat(llm): cover OpenAI streaming usage and split cache tokens; add tests

Addresses review on #1780:
- Enable stream_usage for OpenAI-family models so streaming reports usage
  (LangChain does not emit usage_metadata for ChatOpenAI without it). Verified
  live: gpt-5.4-mini now reports input=21/output=11 where it reported nothing.
- Report cache-read and cache-creation tokens on their own counters (disjoint
  from fresh input) since providers bill them at different rates; captured from
  the Anthropic native, OpenAI Responses, and LangChain paths.
- Log suppressed reporting failures via debug instead of a silent pass.
- Add unit tests for report_llm_tokens and the usage/cache split.

* fix(llm): report token usage from the finally so partial-stream failures still bill

Move report_llm_tokens into the finally of both native adapters
(NativeAnthropicAdapter, NativeOpenAIResponsesAdapter) so a mid-stream error
after message_start/message_delta still records the provider-reported usage.
Adds a regression test that raises mid-stream and asserts the partial usage
(input + cache) was recorded.

* fix(llm): capture usage on failed OpenAI Responses terminal events

response.failed can carry a usage object; read usage on failed/error terminal
events (not only response.completed) so a failed-but-chargeable request reports
tokens instead of zero. finish_reason stays 'error'. Adds a regression test.

* fix(llm): treat response.incomplete as a terminal event in the OpenAI Responses adapter

OpenAI Responses can emit response.incomplete separately from response.completed
(e.g. max_output_tokens). Handle it as terminal: read its usage and map
incomplete_details.reason to finish_reason, so a truncated-but-chargeable request
still records tokens instead of zero. Adds a regression test.

* fix(llm): capture LangChain token usage for every provider, not just OpenAI

The stream_usage gate matched 'OpenAI' in the class name, so ChatXAI never
asked for usage and silently reported none, even though it inherits the flag
from BaseChatOpenAI; ChatBedrock does not declare the field at all. Gate on the
declared flag instead. Report from a finally as well, so a stream that breaks
mid-way still records the usage its chunks already carried, matching the two
native adapters.

* feat(llm): surface per-call token usage in the pipeline Trace

report_llm_tokens publishes each call's usage on a ContextVar; the LLM
node hangs it on Answer.tokens, which the Trace 'Tokens' grid already
renders. One hook at the shared Adapter seam covers every provider.

* fix(llm): accumulate per-turn token usage with a per-call breakdown for the Trace

The counters and the llm_tokens event stay per-call (billing path unchanged), but
the context var feeding answer.tokens now sums every model call in the turn and
carries calls plus a breakdown listing each call's token cost. A ReAct/CrewAI turn
that hits the model N times shows the whole turn's total and what each call cost in
the Trace and action history, instead of only the last call.

* fix(trace): render per-call token breakdown instead of crashing on the object

The Tokens grid mapped answer.tokens as flat scalars; the new per-call breakdown
(an array of objects) made React throw 'Objects are not valid as a React child'.
Split the scalar totals (rendered as chips) from breakdown (one row per model call)
and type answer.tokens as TokenUsage.

* fix(agent): carry per-turn token usage onto the agent's answer

The Trace "Tokens" grid renders answer.tokens, but that field was only ever set
by the LLM node's own questions-lane path. An agent emits its own Answer from
AgentBase.run_agent, so every agentic run reached the Trace with no usage at all
— the case report_llm_tokens' calls/breakdown accumulation was written for.

Read the same context var here and attach it when present. Covers all five
agent frameworks, since they share this base.

* feat(trace): show each model call's tokens on its own invoke row

An 11-call agent run listed 11 breakdown blocks under the answer, none of them
tied to the call that produced them. The data was only ever aggregated onto the
final answer, which also arrives after every invoke has already rendered.

ask() now attaches its own slice of the turn — the breakdown entries appended
while it ran — so each Anthropic INVOKE row shows what that call cost, through
the renderer the row already uses. The answer keeps the turn total and drops the
per-call list.

* fix(llm): thread- and nesting-safe turn usage collector; cover the review findings

Replace the per-turn ContextVar with a module-global, lock-guarded usage collector
scoped by turn_usage(). A ContextVar could not carry usage back from CrewAI/deepagent
kickoffs, which run on a worker thread under contextvars.copy_context() — the agent's
answer showed no tokens (dylan #3). The collector spans threads like the metrics
singleton, and a seen-mark slice makes it nesting-safe: an agent can drive sub-agents,
each its own scope, while the outermost scope reads the whole turn and clears the list
so it stays bounded to one turn (asclearuc/dylan #2).

Also from the reviews:
- reasoning stream (try_openai_compat_reasoning_stream) now asks for include_usage,
  reads the usage-bearing final chunk, and reports on success — it billed zero before
  (dylan #1). It falls back to non-streaming if a strict proxy rejects the flag.
- do not force stream_usage on a custom base URL (vLLM/proxies 400); usage is still
  read if the endpoint sends it (dylan #4).
- drop the per-call metrics.event that fed an unbounded, cumulatively re-serialized
  events list (dylan #5); the counters carry the billable totals.
- correct the max()-vs-additive comment (asclearuc/dylan #6).

Tests: turn total, per-invoke slice, bounding, cross-thread, nested sub-agents, and
no bleed between consecutive turns.

* test(trace): cover the answer Tokens grid render

Per the review: pin that the per-call breakdown is dropped from the chip grid, a
tokens object holding only a breakdown renders no Tokens section, and the non-numeric
model chip is stringified. Follows the media_renderers.test.tsx harness (node --import
tsx --test via shared:test).

* test(llm): assert no per-call event is emitted (it was dropped for O(N^2))

test_emits_llm_tokens_event_payload asserted the per-call llm_tokens metrics.event
that this branch removed. Flip it: the event must NOT be emitted; the counters carry
the totals.

* fix(llm): per-turn usage collector safe under concurrent turns

Move the turn collector from a module global to a ContextVar holding a
mutable list appended in place. Overlapping turns (tool waves, one pipeline
per message) each get their own list, so a Trace never shows another turn's
tokens and the list dies with its scope (no global clear, no unbounded
growth under load). copy_context() shares the list object, so worker-thread
kickoffs still land in the open turn; run the rocketride tool wave under
copy_context().run so its calls propagate.

Meter the whole OpenAI-compatible family: ask for streaming usage on both
the LangChain and native reasoning paths and retry once without the flag if
the endpoint rejects it before the first chunk, instead of hard-disabling it
for every custom base URL (xAI, DeepSeek, Qwen, Together, Groq, vLLM). An
explicit stream_usage in stream_kwargs overrides the default.

Cover the native reasoning capture point and the concurrent-turn, worker-
thread and retry paths with tests.

* fix(llm): isolate sibling invoke scopes; gate + log the LangChain usage retry

Each turn_usage scope now owns its own list and folds it into the parent on
exit, so two invokes running concurrently in one turn (a parallel tool wave)
no longer cross-read each other's per-call breakdown in the Trace; the turn
total is unchanged.

On the LangChain usage-flag retry, warn before retrying (matching the native
path) and gate it on status_code == 400 so a 401/429 surfaces without a
second round trip, while a provider whose error carries no status_code keeps
the broad retry.

* fix(llm): gate the usage-flag retry to real 400s; stop reasoning-only double-bill

Retry without stream_options only on a 400 (the flag rejection), on both the
LangChain and native reasoning paths. A 401/429 or a transient connection
error (no status_code) now re-raises / falls back instead of being retried
without the flag: no silent unmetered success, and a rate limit stays at two
round trips instead of four.

On the reasoning path, report captured usage before the empty-content check
and return the empty answer (the caller keeps it, since it tests `is not
None`), so a reasoning-only turn is not discarded and re-issued via the
non-streaming fallback — which billed the provider twice, metered once. Only
a stream that produced nothing at all still falls back.

* test(llm): cover the LLMBase token seams; widen the usage-flag retry to 4xx

writeQuestions and ask both hang the turn's usage on the Answer and neither had a
test — the plain llm_* node lane. Adds three, including a second ask on the same
instance not inheriting the first's tokens.

The usage-flag retry gated on status 400 only, so a FastAPI-based endpoint (vLLM's
OpenAI-compatible server) answering 422 lost token-by-token streaming on every
request. Both call sites now share is_usage_flag_rejection: any 4xx except
401/403/408/429.

Drops the unused `seen` offset from usage_since (now aggregate_usage) — scopes
isolate by owning their list, and the docstring still taught the replaced design.
Barriers in the concurrency tests get a timeout so a dead thread fails instead of
hanging.

* fix(llm): keep the fallback for a stream that produced nothing

include_usage is now always requested, so usage is set on essentially every
successful stream — and gating the fallback on `usage is None` made it
unreachable. A stream that emits neither content nor reasoning (a proxy that
strips delta.reasoning_content, hitting max_tokens while reasoning) returned
the empty string, which chat.py serves as the answer instead of re-issuing
the request non-streaming.

The usage report already runs before the guard, so ordering alone keeps the
stream metered once; the fallback's own metering covers the second request,
which the provider bills anyway.

Also hang the turn's usage on the error answer: the adapters report from
their finally, so the tokens are known — without this the Trace grid is
empty for exactly the turn a user opens.

* feat(llm): meter the five drivers that bypass the Adapter capture point

LangChainAdapter meters every provider that routes through ChatBase, but five
drivers override that seam and reach their SDK directly, so the Adapter never
sees them and they billed zero. Two seams are overridden: _chat (gemini,
ibm_watson, minimax) and the chat seam above it (perplexity, mistral).

Gemini is the widest gap: it sets _client and never _llm, so the streaming gate
in chat.py is never true and every call — streaming or not — took the override.

Each now reports from its own call site, off its SDK's own usage object, keeping
the four counters disjoint: Gemini counts prompt_token_count with the cached
prefix included (subtracted back out) and bills thoughts_token_count as output;
watsonx and Mistral carry no cache detail. _report_usage_metadata is now public
so the two LangChain-backed drivers reuse the shared split instead of copying it.

Also covers the error-path answer.tokens seam on LLMBase, which landed in
17ce15ea without a test.

The four llm_vision_* nodes and accessibility_describe override the same chat
seam and stay unmetered: they are image-priced, so they need their own
accounting decision rather than a copy of this one.

* fix(llm): never let a usage read cost the user the answer they paid for

The usage split runs before report_llm_tokens' own guard, so a provider or proxy
answering a non-numeric count raised out of the metering code and into the
caller — which is a retry loop. Verified against the real driver: a successful,
already-billed Perplexity response came back to the user as "Perplexity API
error: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'n/a'".

report_usage_metadata was already exposed to this before the five drivers were
wired to it (LangChainAdapter.collect() calls it on every non-streaming turn);
the new call sites widened the same hole to five more providers.

Guards the split in report_usage_metadata and in the three SDK readers, sharing
one debug_usage_failure() so every capture point fails the same way — the trace
loses that call's tokens, the turn keeps its answer. One regression test per
driver.

* refactor(llm): drop the redundant usage guard in the two pass-through readers

report_llm_tokens coerces its own arguments inside its own try and reports the
failure through the same debug_usage_failure, so the local try in the watson and
mistral readers could not change the outcome. Pass the raw values through: a
missing count still reads as zero, a non-numeric one is swallowed one frame
deeper, and the per-driver regression test holds.

llm_gemini keeps its guard — it subtracts and adds the counts before calling.

* feat(nodes): add the Scan Cropper node (#2014)

Splits a scan holding several photographs into one image per photograph,
straightened, cropped to its own edges, and named in reading order. The text lane
carries a JSON detection record: what was found, where, and what it was called.

Background is inferred from the scan rather than configured. A pixel counts as
background only when it is plain, painted in one of the scan's dominant colours,
and part of a region reaching the scan edge — each condition covers a gap the
others leave. Photos mounted edge to edge are separated by cutting along straight
borders that span a region, with standard print ratios arbitrating the cut as a
veto rather than a requirement, so panoramas survive.

Detection runs on a downscaled copy and the rectangles are scaled back up, which
is what makes a 143 MP flatbed scan tractable; the crops themselves are always cut
at full resolution.

Names are dense: a photo detected but not cropped leaves no gap in the numbering,
because a gap reads as lost data. The `cropped` flag in the record finds those
instead. The counter runs per object, so an upstream fan-out still gets unique
names. A scan yielding nothing is forwarded unchanged rather than dropped.

Configuration is by scan type, not by raw numbers, and each preset opens its own
advanced panel filled with that preset's values — so tuning starts from the
nearest case rather than from ten blank fields.

`source_quality` and `matched_quality` move into `ai.common.utils`: they recover
the quality a JPEG was written at and choose one to re-encode with, need only the
standard library, and the orientation node wants the first of them too.

The detection algorithm, the seam search and the quality tables come from the
author's personal forks of `autocrop` and `ScanCropper`, contributed here by their
author under this repository's MIT licence.

* fix(scan_cropper): address review of the node

A scan whose regions were all found but none cut left the image lane with
nothing: the fallback was gated on the detections rather than on what was
actually emitted, so regions too small to cut, or that failed to encode, dropped
the object from the lane entirely. It now forwards the original whenever no crop
went out.

`cropped` was set inside the crop loop, which runs only when something listens on
the image lane. A text-only wiring therefore produced regions without the key at
all, and a consumer reading it failed with `KeyError` on that wiring alone. It is
set where the region is built, so the audit record has one shape.

`float('inf')` parses and `int()` on it raises `OverflowError`, which is not a
`ValueError` and escaped the quality-config handler into `beginGlobal`.

`source_quality` mis-read fill bytes: a JPEG may pad with any number of 0xFF
before a marker code, and reading one as a code took the next two bytes for a
segment length and put the scan out of step for the rest of the file. The
quantisation table was then never found and crops were written at the default
quality instead of the matched one. Marker 0x01 carries no payload and was
mis-parsed the same way.

`connectedComponents` takes connectivity by keyword — the second positional
parameter is the output `labels`. OpenCV accepts the scalar and the default
connectivity is 8, so the result was right, but the call read as something it
was not.

The stream helper in the tests caught every exception, so a failure raised out of
`_finish` looked like a clean run — and the tests that assert nothing was emitted
would have passed on a node that crashed. It now swallows only
`Ec.PreventDefault`. Adds the missing case: regions detected, no crops emitted.

* test(scan_cropper): cover the detector core

Every existing test stubs `split_scan` out, so nothing reached `find_photos`, the
seam search or `dedupe`. Only the single declarative `count == 3` case touched any
of it, and a regression in the separation logic would have passed.

Synthetic scans rather than fixtures: an image on disk pins one photograph of one
album, while a generated page states the property being tested. The pair that
matters is two prints mounted edge to edge with only a tonal step between them —
two regions with the seam search, one with `maxDepth 0`. Same image, same code,
and the setting the README calls the main speed lever is the only thing deciding
the outcome.

Also covered: a hairline of paper between prints, a blank page, specks under
`minArea`, an over-long strip rejected by `maxAspect`, `dedupe` on an overlapping
pair and on a disjoint one, and `snap_to_border` declining below its size floor.
Sizes are compared with a tolerance, never pixel for pixel — where an edge lands
depends on the noise that painted the photograph.

One case is not about separation at all: detection runs downscaled while crops are
cut at full size, so a small `detect_size` run is compared against one that did not
downscale. Losing the scale-up would take a third-size corner out of every photo.

This covers the detector's plumbing, not its judgement. Whether it finds the right
rectangles on a real album page remains the declarative case and the manual run.

* fix(scan_cropper): fall back on a config value that is not a finite number

`_number` caught `TypeError` and `ValueError`, the same pair `resolve_quality`
caught before it was widened. `int(float('inf'))` raises `OverflowError`, which is
neither, so an infinite value on `detectSize` or `maxDepth` escaped the fallback
and failed the node in `beginGlobal` — the one outcome these functions exist to
prevent.

Underneath that sat the quieter half. `OverflowError` only fires on the integer
fields; on a float field `float('inf')` succeeds, and `nan` succeeds everywhere.
Neither is stopped by the clamp, because every comparison against `nan` is false
and `max(low, min(high, nan))` hands it straight back. It then reaches
`DetectParams`, and each threshold that reads it becomes a no-op — detection goes
strange rather than failing. Both are rejected after the cast now.

Adds tests for the config layer, which had none: `_number` over good, missing,
out-of-range, non-numeric and non-finite values; `_params_from_config` showing one
poisoned field costs only itself; and `resolve_quality` across text, JSON numbers,
clamping and the non-finite forms.

* fix(scan_cropper): reject a boolean where a number was expected

`bool` subclasses `int`, so `int(True)` is 1 and a config carrying
`"maxDepth": true` passed the cast, the finite check and the clamp, arriving in
`DetectParams` as 1. The node would then cut a blob apart once instead of the
documented four times, and say nothing — the same shape of failure as `nan`, a
different setting rather than a crash.

The test has to sit before the cast; afterwards there is nothing left to tell
`True` from `1`. This is the rule `_avi_declared_size` already applies when it
reads a declared stream size.

* test(scan_cropper): derive the tunable list instead of spelling it out

`test_every_tunable_survives_a_config_of_rubbish` listed eight field names where
`_params_from_config` fills nine, so `ratioTolerance` was never fed a bad value
and the test claimed more than it checked.

Adding the missing name would leave the same trap for the next tunable. The
rubbish config is built from `_RANGES` now, and the assertion walks
`dataclasses.fields`, so both ends follow the code they are testing.

… (#1861)

* fix(guardrails): stop delivering every answer/question/document twice

writeAnswers/writeQuestions/writeDocuments all forwarded explicitly on every
non-blocked path but never called preventDefault(), so the engine's own
default forward ran afterward too -- every item was delivered twice
downstream, independent of enable_hallucination_check or policy_mode (warn
vs log). Same bug class as #1638 (memory_persistent double-forwarding).

preventDefault() raises immediately (rocketlib's real implementation is
`raise APERR(Ec.PreventDefault, ...)`), so it has to run AFTER the explicit
forward, not before, or the forward itself would never execute. Added
_forward_question/_forward_answer helpers that do both in the correct order;
writeDocuments gets the same treatment inline since it has only one path.

Added TestIInstanceDeliveredExactlyOnce, which simulates the engine's actual
dispatch mechanism (call the override; unless it raised PreventDefault, also
invoke the engine's default forward) so the assertion is "delivered exactly
once end-to-end" rather than just "IInstance's own forward call happened
once" -- the latter would not have caught this bug.

Fixes #1849

* test(nodes): measure the double-delivery fix against a running engine

The unit tests re-state the engine's default-forward rule in Python. If that
assumption were wrong they would be wrong in the same direction and still
pass. This measures the rule instead: the same payload runs through two real
pipelines, one with guardrails in the chain and one without, and the response
sink counts the deliveries. The sink appends one entry per write, so the entry
count is the forward count. The baseline is asserted first, so a wrong count
can never be blamed on the source.

All three forwarding lanes are covered. Questions and documents are injected
straight onto the lane with a `lane/<name>` MIME, so no model and no network
is involved. Answers come from `llm_openai_api` under `ROCKETRIDE_MOCK`,
because `Answer` rejects a preset `answer` field during validation - an
injected answer would arrive empty and take the early-return path instead of
the evaluated one.

Each run terminates its pipeline. Two pipelines per test left registered piled
up live tasks on the shared server, which surfaced as a refused connection on
a later `pipe.open()` under xdist.

Checked with `builder nodes:test`: 3 passed on three consecutive runs, and 3
failed on the count assertion with the guardrails change reverted.

* feat(nodes): add the Image Orientation Fixer node (#2015)

Turns scanned photographs the right way up. Each image is examined four ways — as
it arrived and turned 90, 180, 270 — faces are detected in each, and the
orientation they agree on wins. The text lane carries the decision: what was
chosen, how sure it was, and, when it declined, which doubt stopped it.

A photograph turned the wrong way is worse than one left alone, so safety comes
from a rule rather than a threshold: two independent readings of the same
detections must point the same way. One asks which orientation holds the most
face, the other which the detector was most certain about. Where they disagree the
node abstains. Deciding on one reading alone was measured and turned two
photographs wrongly at the same coverage.

An image that is not rotated is forwarded byte for byte, never re-encoded, so
abstaining costs nothing in quality. Formats other than JPEG and PNG are analysed
and reported but never re-saved: their original compression settings cannot be
recovered, and choosing one silently is worse than declining.

Defaults are measurements, not guesses — 98 album photographs, 37 corrected, none
turned the wrong way — and the README states the trade for each dial so the
setting can be chosen against a number.

The detector is YuNet, MIT licensed, pinned by URL and SHA-256 and cached after
first use. It arrives through `ai.common.opencv`, so the node adds no package;
MediaPipe BlazeFace would have pulled in a framework for the same job.

* fix(image_orient): address review of the node

Two guarantees held on one path each, which in both cases was the rarer one.

A tie between two rotations was decided rather than declined. `margin` bottoms
out at 1.0 and the form offers that value first, so `ratio < margin` stopped
being a threshold exactly where users are most likely to set it: two rotations
scoring alike passed the check, and the winner came from their position in the
sort order. A photograph could be re-encoded at 90 degrees on no evidence for 90
degrees, which is the one outcome this node is built to avoid. A tie abstains now.

The pinned checksum was verified only on the download that created the cache.
Every later run — that is, nearly all of them — returned the cached file because
it existed, so the pin guaranteed nothing beyond the first start on a machine.
The cache is hashed before use, and replaced when it does not match. Hashing
230 KB costs less than a millisecond, so the guarantee becomes permanent for
nothing.

The fetch itself was unbounded in both time and size: `urlretrieve` takes no
timeout, and this runs in `beginGlobal`, so an endpoint that accepts a connection
and sends nothing hangs node startup rather than failing. Bounded at 30 seconds
and 32 MB, both far above a 230 KB model.

Two README claims were wrong. It advised lowering the margin "toward 1.5" when
the default is 1.1, which is a rise described as a fall; and it said the record
tells you which way an unencodable image should go, while the code resets
`rotation` to 0 and reports only `unencodable_format`.

* feat(ai,mcp): OAuth 2.0 discovery and audience enforcement for /mcp

Claude and ChatGPT cannot be handed an API key — they only authenticate via
OAuth. Make /mcp a spec-compliant OAuth 2.0 protected resource so they can
discover how to log in, and check that the tokens they come back with were
actually issued for MCP.

Discovery (RFC 9728):
- Serve the protected-resource metadata document publicly at
  /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp, naming Zitadel as the
  authorization server. It has to be public — it is what an unauthenticated
  client reads in order to learn how to authenticate.
- Advertise it from WWW-Authenticate on 401s, scoped to the MCP resource so
  unrelated engine routes do not misdirect clients.

Audience enforcement:
- Verify the JWT signature against the issuer's JWKS, check the issuer, and
  require MCP_EXPECTED_AUDIENCE to appear in aud. Bearer tokens are
  interchangeable, so without this a token minted for the VS Code extension
  would open /mcp just as readily as one minted for Claude.
- Static API keys (rr_/tk_/pk_/cd_) keep the existing path untouched.
- Credentials that are neither a known key prefix nor a decodable JWT are
  refused while enforcing. Zitadel can be configured to issue opaque access
  tokens, which would otherwise be mistaken for API keys and bypass the
  audience check entirely.
- An unset audience is tolerated on a loopback bind and refused on any other,
  mirroring MCP_DEV_NO_AUTH: local development keeps working, while a deploy
  that forgets the setting fails loudly instead of silently accepting every
  token it is handed.
- Close websocket scopes at the mount. AuthMiddleware is a BaseHTTPMiddleware
  and only wraps 'http' scopes, but Mount routes by path for any scope type,
  so a websocket would otherwise reach the session manager unauthenticated.

The audience check lives at the /mcp boundary rather than in the engine's
global authenticator chain on purpose: "was this token issued for MCP" is a
rule about MCP, and must not be imposed on /task or /api/chat.

excludes new files under packages/ai/tests/.

requested redirect_uri is missing in the client configuration" for everyone.

esbuild.js inlines RR_ZITADEL_VSCODE_CLIENT_ID at build time and it is the

cursor:// both return 302.

`Store.read_bytes` falls back to `read_file()` and re-encodes via
latin-1. `read_file` on S3 UTF-8 decodes the object body, so every
binary read raises UnicodeDecodeError before the caller sees a byte.
Only the filesystem provider overrides these; S3, Azure and memory
all inherit the text round-trip.

This is why app deploy fails on staging and works locally: local
runs use the filesystem store. The `materialize` phase reads back
the retained transport zip and dies on the local-file-header:

    retained transport zip unreadable: Failed to read file
    .../bundle/<app>-v000001.zip from S3: 'utf-8' codec can't
    decode byte 0xe9 in position 10: invalid continuation byte

Verified against the real object in the staging bucket: it is a
valid archive (PK\x03\x04, 11 entries), so the upload path was
never at fault. The old code path reproduces the byte offset above
exactly; the new one opens the zip.

`write_bytes` is overridden alongside it. The stored
`remoteEntry.js` objects are pure ASCII, where latin-1 and UTF-8
agree, so no existing object changes meaning.

* fix(store): retry the transport failures boto actually raises

Every retry decorator in the S3 provider matched only the builtin
ConnectionError and TimeoutError. botocore inherits from neither:

    EndpointConnectionError  builtin ConnectionError = False
    ConnectTimeoutError      builtin ConnectionError = False
    ReadTimeoutError         builtin ConnectionError = False

So a real S3 transport failure fell through to the bare
`except Exception`, was wrapped in StorageError, and Tenacity never
saw it. The retry logic in this file had never retried the failure
it was written for -- 9 decorators and 9 except clauses, all of them
matching something boto does not raise.

Replaces both with one TRANSIENT_ERRORS tuple so the decorator and
the pass-through except can no longer disagree about what counts as
transient.

The botocore import is GUARDED. store_providers/__init__ imports
S3Store unconditionally, so this module loads on filesystem-store
installs that never had boto3; _get_client() gives those a readable
error at call time, and a hard import would replace it with an
ImportError at import time. Verified in a subprocess with botocore
blocked: the module imports and the tuple falls back to the two
builtins.

EndpointResolutionError is deliberately excluded. It is nearly always
a misconfigured region or endpoint, and retrying a config error only
delays the message explaining it.

Closes #2115

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_015nTVr6jfSFYm1GppxbjghP

* fix(store): the compare-and-swap site was still on the literal tuple

One site escaped the first pass, and it is the exact bug this PR
exists to fix. The conditional-write method carries a THREE-element
tuple:

    retry_if_exception_type((ConnectionError, TimeoutError, _RaceConditionError))
    except (ConnectionError, TimeoutError, self._RaceConditionError):

My grep matched the two-element literal, so the third element hid
both from it. The result would have shipped a provider where every
S3 operation retries real transport failures EXCEPT the conditional
write -- the one where a transient mid-CAS failure most deserves
another attempt.

Now TRANSIENT_ERRORS + (_RaceConditionError,) in both places, so the
race-condition retry composes with the transport set instead of
replacing it.

Found by @anandray in review. The instrument answered a narrower
question than I asked it: "find the literal tuple" is not "find every
place that decides what counts as transient".

… uv resolve (#2126)

* feat(depends): cache the satisfied verdict so cold processes skip the uv resolve

`_processed` only spans one process, so every cold engine process re-ran the
uv dry-run for each requirements file and, on a warm machine, only learned
that everything was already installed — 20-40s behind the engine-global lock.

Persist that verdict under <engine cache>/satisfied/, one file per
requirements file, keyed by everything the resolve consults: the requirements
file, the compiled constraints/overrides/excludes, the interpreter and the
installed dist-info set. A matching key skips the dry-run and the install; any
change reruns them. Lock semantics are unchanged.

Fixes #2089

* fix(depends): fingerprint files pulled in through -r/-c in the verdict key

A change inside an included requirements file left the verdict key unchanged (CodeRabbit on #2126). The key now digests the full include closure, resolved relative to each including file; adds regression tests and docstrings on the new tests.

* fix(depends): join backslash-continued lines before scanning requirement includes

pip and uv treat a trailing backslash as a line continuation, so a continued -r/-c directive was invisible to _requirements_closure (CodeRabbit on #2126). Join continuations before matching; adds a regression test.

* fix(depends): treat an unreadable or unwritable verdict cache as a miss, never a failure

_save_verdict runs on the success path, so an OSError from the cache directory turned a successful resolve or install into a failed depends(); the read side had the same hole via _load_stored_hash. Both are now best-effort, like the progress sidecar (CodeRabbit on #2126).

* fix(depends): never cache a verdict the key cannot compute honestly

Review on #2126 found two ways the cache fails wrong. A non-UTF-8 included file raised UnicodeDecodeError out of _requirements_closure and hard-failed node startup — new, since an included file was previously read only by uv. And an include path with a space captured a name that does not exist, so the real file was never fingerprinted and an edit to it kept a satisfied verdict: a silent stale hit. The decode is now replace-on-error, quoted paths parse, and _verdict_key returns None whenever an input is invisible to it, which degrades to resolving every time. Adds _VERDICT_SCHEMA so a change to the resolve's own arguments retires old verdicts, and makes --rebuild-cache clear the verdicts so a bad state is recoverable without a redeploy.

* fix(depends): refuse the key when site-packages cannot be listed

_installed_fingerprint hashed an empty list on OSError, which is a stable digest — the key would stop noticing installs and every verdict would stay satisfied for ever. It now returns None and _verdict_key refuses, so the failure degrades to resolving. bootstrap() creates the directory before any key is computed, so this cannot fire on the real path.

* fix(depends): verify the verdict cache was actually cleared, and gate on isfile

--rebuild-cache reported a cleared cache even when the directory survived: removeDir returns false and only warns when it is in use (EPERM/EBUSY), so a surviving verdict left depends() skipping the re-resolve the flag exists to force (CodeRabbit on #2126). The task now confirms the directory is gone and fails loudly if it is not, checked on the directory rather than on removeDir's return value, which reports success for an absent directory too. Also takes the review's note that _verdict_key gated on os.path.exists, so an include naming a directory passed the gate and then digested to '' - a stable key over an unreadable input, the shape the refusal exists to prevent.
