* feat(mcp): add resolve_config, showing what a node actually receives

A .pipe rarely says what a node gets. The engine merges profile defaults and,
when a profile is set, reads the user layer only from the sub-object named after
that profile, so a key written beside it is discarded in silence. The author of
#1989 lost a day to exactly that, and the schema cannot express it: a schema
describes what a field is, not that this field in this profile will be dropped.

resolve_config runs the config through the same Config.getNodeConfig a node calls
at load, and returns the resolved result plus the keys the resolver discarded,
with a hint naming the object they belong in.

Resolution has to happen engine-side. getServiceSchemas copies 15 keys into the
catalog and preconfig is not among them (services.cpp:2100-2148), so profile
resolution cannot be reproduced from rrext_services or /services.

The tool reaches the engine through the existing seam rather than importing
Config directly. modules/mcp/engine.py states that tools depend only on the
EngineClient protocol so a later revision can swap the WS SDK for in-process
calls without touching tool code; a direct import would have made this the first
tool to break that. So this adds rrext_resolve_config next to rrext_services and
rrext_validate, the matching SDK method, and one line on each side of the seam.

Both argument checks default only a genuinely absent config: `or {}` would
coerce a falsy non-object such as [] and skip the type check entirely. A test
caught that.

doc.md gains the tool row and its count moves to 28.

* feat(mcp): add scaffold_node, emitting a node that loads on the first try

Authoring a node means discovering its contract by failure, and the documented
contract is wrong in three places, so reading the docs first does not help:

- preconfig is marked optional in README-node-schema.md, but
  Config.getNodeConfig raises without it and nearly every IGlobal calls that at
  load. Of 170 services*.json in the tree, the only ones without preconfig are
  global-field files with no protocol plus a handful whose IGlobal never calls
  it.
- depends() is documented as running in __init__.py, and the same page then
  contradicts itself. The real nodes call it from IGlobal.beginGlobal, and any
  third-party import has to follow it.
- The "Adding a New Node" example shows a plain class with a process() method,
  which nothing in the engine calls. The contract is IGlobalBase/IInstanceBase.

Two more the docs omit: a services.json without protocol is not registered as a
service at all, and register must be filter or endpoint or the node loads but
can never be instantiated. The provider name is the protocol, which is the
mistake the issue opens with.

scaffold_node emits all of that correctly, including the parent
local_nodes/__init__.py and the local_nodes.<name> import path. class_type and
lane_out are checked against the live catalog rather than a list here, so the
allowed sets follow the engine instead of drifting as nodes are added.

It returns files rather than writing them. _common.load_pipeline already refuses
server-side reads because an MCP caller could otherwise reach the server's disk;
writing deserves the same stance.

The tests assert the emitted skeleton against the engine's real requirements:
every generated Python file parses, the manifest carries the four keys that stop
a node loading, depends() is in IGlobal and not __init__.py, and the handler
matches the requested lane. Dropping preconfig from the template fails them.

doc.md gains the tool row and its count moves to 29.

* fix(client-python): let a non-object config reach the engine's type check

resolve_config defaulted with `config or {}`, which coerces a falsy non-object
such as [] into {} and hides the mistake the engine would have reported. Only an
absent config is defaulted now, matching the handler it calls.

* fix(mcp): report a config key the profile overwrote, not just an absent one

resolve_config decided a key was discarded by checking whether it was missing
from the resolved config. Nearly every profile in the catalog declares apikey,
so an apikey written beside "profile" comes back present, holding the profile's
value rather than the author's, and the tool stayed silent on the exact case it
exists to surface.

A key now counts as discarded when what the node receives differs from what the
author wrote. Found by calling the tool over the MCP transport against a real
llm_openai profile; the unit test missed it because its stub returned a resolved
config without the key at all.

* refactor(mcp): give the catalog lookups one job each

_catalog_values branched on whether its key argument was the string 'lanes',
so one function carried two different traversals. Splitting them drops the
branch and the stringly-typed parameter, and the lane names are now filtered
for strings the way the class types already were.

* fix(mcp): harden scaffold_node against catalog and argument shapes

Three defects found in review:

A catalog entry whose classType is a bare string was iterated character by
character, so 'text' admitted 't', 'e' and 'x' as class types and rejected the
real one. Introduced when the lookup was split in two; the container check that
guarded it is back.

Dispatch does not apply the tool's inputSchema, so a non-string name reached the
regex and raised TypeError instead of returning an actionable answer. Name, both
lanes and class_type are now checked for type first.

lane_in was validated only against the local handler templates, never against
the catalog, so a lane with a template but no engine support produced a manifest
with an input lane nothing serves.

Also corrects the introspection group heading in doc.md, which still counted 5
tools and did not list scaffold.py as a source.

* fix(mcp): report every profile sibling key, not only one whose value changed

Comparing the resolved value against the author's missed the sibling that
happens to match the profile's own value. The resolver never read that line
either, so staying quiet left the author believing it was in effect when the
key inside the profile is what applied.

With a profile set every sibling is discarded, so the value is not worth
comparing and the check is simpler for it.

* fix(mcp): keep a supplied falsy argument out of the scaffold defaults

lane_in, lane_out and class_type defaulted with `or`, so a supplied 0, '' or []
became the fallback and never reached the type check that would have reported
it. Defaulting now applies only to an absent or null argument, matching the
handler this PR already corrected on the client side.

* feat(mcp): flag a component whose provider the engine cannot serve

validate_pipeline passed a pipeline naming a provider that does not exist, so a
typed name validated clean and failed later at run time. The engine's provider
lookup lives in validate_pipeline.cpp's single-component path, which the whole
pipeline path never reaches.

The tool now checks each component against the engine's service catalog after
the engine's own validation, and reports the component id with the name it could
not resolve. The names come from the engine, so no rule moves into the client,
and engine findings are added to rather than replaced.

Closes the third of the four tools #1989 asked for; it was previously treated as
already shipped in #1880, which covers the structural half only.

* fix(mcp): report only the config keys a profile actually discarded

resolve_config reported every sibling of the selected profile, so it named
parameters on all 34 components in the repo's own pipelines that select one,
and told the author to move it inside the profile object. parameters is not
node configuration: the engine validates and consumes it on its own path
(pipeline_config.cpp Rule 5 and Rule 6), and moving it would break the
component. name is the same shape, and an editor-saved config keeps a
sub-object per profile, so an unselected profile read as a discarded key too.

Structural keys and the service's own profile names are now excluded. Over the
same pipelines the report goes from 34 components to 1, and that one is a real
finding: search_exa carries apikey beside the profile.

The existing test passed because its config was hand-written with only apikey
beside the profile. The new one is shaped like a real .pipe.

Also drops the return in the scaffolded handler's preventDefault call, which
raises, matching how the real nodes write it.

* fix(examples): repair the two component configs these tools surfaced

Both are real defects the PR's own additions found in shipped examples.

document-processor names provider "anonymize", but that node declares
"protocol": "anonymize_text://" and the provider is the protocol minus the
scheme, so no such service exists and the component could never instantiate.
The new provider check in validate_pipeline flags it; the old validator
resolved the definition and silently ignored the miss.

exa-search-working carries apikey beside "profile", where getNodeConfig never
reads it, so the pipe named "working" resolved its key to the profile's empty
default. Moving it inside the profile object is correct under the current
resolver and under the one #2039 and #1979 propose. resolve_config reports it.

Over every pipeline in the repo, resolve_config now reports no discarded keys.

* fix(ai,client-python,client-typescript): give task failures a machine-readable code

A dead task token was indistinguishable from a live one: every task lookup
failure raised a bare RuntimeError, and the only signal a client had was the
English sentence, so applications matched on prose that a reword or a
translation would silently break. The SDKs then appended a developer
troubleshooting checklist to that message, which reached end users verbatim.

Engine: a TaskError carrying a code (TASK_NOT_REGISTERED, TASK_AMBIGUOUS,
TASK_COMPLETED, TASK_STOPPED) at the registry lookups and the readiness wait.
It subclasses RuntimeError and the messages are unchanged, so existing handling
and existing string matches keep working.

Protocol: DAPBase.build_exception copies a string `code` off the exception onto
the DAP error packet, next to `message`. Additive — a plain exception still
produces a byte-identical packet.

SDKs: `code` and `hint` on DAPException (optional readonly fields in
TypeScript, properties in Python), and DataPipe.open() keeps the server's
message as the message with the checklist moved to `hint`.

The old test passed an undefined question, which trips chat()'s empty-question guard before a pipe exists — it exercised the catch without reaching the path it names. The stubbed request now rejects with a plain Error from inside open() (CodeRabbit on #2127).

Audited all eight remaining ValueError: docstring claims against each function's actual raise paths rather than fixing an arbitrary subset (CodeRabbit and review on #2127). * fix(models/ocr): use OS trust store for model downloads; route polars via lts-cpu wrapper

- ssl: install truststore and inject it into the default SSL context so
  HTTPS model downloads use the full OS trust store, fixing "unable to get
  local issuer certificate" behind TLS-intercepting proxies (falls back to
  certifi).
- polars: route OCR polars imports through ai.common.polars, which installs
  polars-lts-cpu and removes any transitively-pulled plain polars, fixing
  SIGILL / SEH 0xc000001d on x86_64 hosts without AVX2/FMA.

Fixes #1162

* refactor(models/ocr): lazy SSL injection, lock polars cleanup, fix comments

Address review feedback on the TLS trust-store / polars-lts-cpu fix:

- SSL injection is now lazy and process-scoped to local mode. ai.common.ssl
  exposes an idempotent ensure() guarded by a module-level flag, called from
  BaseLoader._ensure_dependencies (the chokepoint every local load() hits)
  before the per-class requirements guard, instead of running eagerly at
  ai.common.models import. Remote-mode dispatch processes never import ML
  libraries or download weights, so they no longer pay for the injection.
- The polars-lts-cpu cleanup (pip uninstall + force-reinstall) now runs under
  the same install.lock FileLock that depends() uses. pip() runs raw with no
  locking, so concurrent worker startups could otherwise interleave and
  corrupt site-packages mid-rewrite.
- Replace the silent `except: pass` in both shims with debug logging so a
  skipped cleanup/injection is observable.
- Document that the version('polars') check queries the distribution name
  (not the import name), which is why it detects the transitive plain wheel.
- Correct the nodes/ocr/requirements.txt comment: listing polars-lts-cpu does
  not stop a transitive plain `polars` from installing; the runtime cleanup is
  what makes lts-cpu authoritative.
- Note that the kokoro spaCy-wheel `pip install <url>` validates TLS with
  pip's own CA bundle and is not covered by the in-process ssl injection.

* refactor(models): drop polars lts-cpu shim, import engLib directly

B1: the polars AVX2 crash no longer reproduces against currently-resolved
versions, so the wrapper is dropped rather than kept as a permanent shim.

  * img2table resolves to 2.0.0, whose metadata declares no polars
    dependency and whose wheel contains no reference to polars in any
    module, so nothing pulls plain polars in transitively any more.
  * polars 1.43.2 moved its compiled runtime into separate
    polars-runtime-32/64/compat distributions and selects the baseline
    build by default, so the plain wheel no longer requires AVX2.
  * polars-lts-cpu is frozen at 1.33.1, so keeping the pin would hold the
    OCR node ten minor versions behind.
  * the only polars call site, to_ocr_dataframe(), belongs to the
    img2table v1 plug-in contract, which v2 replaced with of(). It is not
    reachable on a fresh install.

ai/common/polars and the ocr requirements pin are removed, and the OCR
node returns to its develop state.

B4: ai.common.ssl imports engLib.debug directly instead of proxying it
behind a try/except no-op. engLib is built into the engine, so the
fallback masked import errors rather than guarding a real absence.

* fix(ai): make the SSL trust store fallback reachable and the guard race-free

- Move depends(requirements) inside the guarded block. It ran before the
  try, so a failed install propagated out of ensure() and the documented
  certifi fallback was never reached.
- Set the one-shot guard after the attempt finishes, under a lock. It was
  set up front, so a second thread could return while the first was still
  injecting and then download weights through an unpatched SSL context.
  A failed attempt is still recorded, so a broken environment is not
  re-run through the install lock on every later load().
- Declare certifi in requirements.txt. The fallback imports it, so it can
  no longer depend on a transitive copy being present. Note truststore's
  Python 3.10+ floor there as well.

* feat(tika): support RAR5 archives via 7-Zip-JBinding

Tika's junrar-backed RarParser throws on RAR v5 (the default WinRAR format
since 2013). Add net.sf.sevenzipjbinding plus a RarSevenZipParser that
auto-detects RAR4/RAR5 and routes entries through the configured
EmbeddedDocumentExtractor; ConfigBuilder swaps the parser and TikaApi
initializes the native binding once per JVM.

Fixes #1163

* refactor(tika): bulk RAR extraction, per-entry encryption handling, ASF header

Address review feedback on the 7-Zip-JBinding RAR parser:

- Replace per-entry extractSlow() with a single IInArchive.extract(int[],
  false, callback) pass. extractSlow re-decompresses from the start of the
  archive on every call, which is O(n^2) on solid RAR archives; the bulk
  call decompresses once while preserving solid-block ordering. Each entry
  is spooled to a temp file and dispatched to the embedded extractor as it
  completes, so peak disk usage stays at one entry.
- Stop aborting the whole archive on the first encrypted entry. Encrypted
  entries are now logged and skipped per-entry, consistent with how
  unreadable headers and failed extractions are handled; an
  EncryptedDocumentException is surfaced only when every entry is encrypted
  (the archive as a whole is unreadable).
- Switch the file's license header from MIT/Aparavi to the Apache ASF
  header used by sibling parsers, since handleEntryMetadata is ported from
  Tika's Apache-2.0 PackageParser.
- Document the frozen sevenzipjbinding 16.02-2.01 security posture in the
  pom alongside the dependency.

* fix(tika): gate the RAR parser swap on 7-Zip init, harden init and cleanup

- ConfigBuilder replaced Tika's RarParser unconditionally, so when the
  7-Zip-JBinding native library failed to load the config removed the only
  working RAR parser and installed one that cannot run. Gate the swap on
  TikaApi.isSevenZipReady() and keep junrar (RAR4) when it is not.
- TikaApi.init() checked and assigned `initialized` without synchronization,
  so two callers could both pass the guard and race into
  initSevenZipFromPlatformJAR(). Make init() synchronized and the flag
  volatile.
- Narrow the init catch from Throwable to Exception | LinkageError. A missing
  or incompatible native library arrives as UnsatisfiedLinkError, which
  LinkageError still covers, while OutOfMemoryError and StackOverflowError now
  propagate instead of being logged and ignored.
- Close and delete the entry still in flight when bulk extraction aborts.
  setOperationResult() handles the normal path, but 7-Zip-JBinding does not
  promise a matching call once a callback throws, and on Windows the open
  handle also stops TemporaryResources from deleting the file.

* fix(sync_models): reject output token values that equal the context window

LiteLLM and OpenRouter report max output tokens as the context window for
some models. That value reaches the provider as max_tokens and the call is
rejected with a 400. Discard such a candidate and try the next source; the
fallback default no longer overwrites a limit already in the catalogue.

Fail the sync when a profile still has modelOutputTokens equal to
modelTotalTokens, and cover every llm_* node with a catalogue test.

* fix(sync_models): scope the output-token check to providers that cap completions

Equality between modelOutputTokens and modelTotalTokens only proves a broken
value where the provider enforces a completion limit below its window. OpenAI
rejects an oversized max_tokens outright and litellm swaps the fields for
Anthropic, so both opt in via output_limit_below_context. Mistral and xAI accept
max_tokens up to the window and publish no separate limit, which is why every
source reports the two values as equal there — applying the check globally would
have replaced correct data with the 4096 default.

The gate now fails only for native profiles on an opted-in provider, skips
deprecated ones and any model confirmed in model_output_tokens.overrides, and
reports the rest as a note.

The four gpt-5-*-chat-latest profiles carried 16384 in both fields, hand-entered.
16384 is their real output limit; the context window was the wrong one — both
models.dev and litellm report 128000 — so the window is corrected instead. They
were also truncating prompts at 16k.

* fix(llm): warn when a custom profile sets max_tokens above what the model accepts

A custom profile carries whatever the author typed and the model sync never
sees it, so nothing catches an oversized max_tokens before the request goes
out. The provider answers with a 400 naming a limit the author never saw, and
by then the value may not even be in the pipeline file any more.

Resolve the configured model name against the node's own catalogue: most custom
profiles name a model that is also a profile there, which gives a real
completion limit to compare against. Anything above it is named with both
numbers. Without a catalogue match, fall back to reporting output equal to the
context window. Catalogue entries whose own output equals their window are
skipped as a comparison basis - that value is the window, not a limit.

* fix(sync_models): check hand-written token limits before the clamp, and keep the sync PR flowing

Review feedback.

The runtime check ran after validate_max_tokens, so a value the provider would
reject could be clamped into a plausible one with nothing left to report. It now
reads what the author wrote. It also keyed off profile == 'custom', which misses
the profile-less direct-config form and llm_openai_api, whose default profile is
'custom' so an omitted key resolves there without the literal ever appearing.
The trigger is now the presence of a hand-supplied token field at either config
level, which is what actually distinguishes an author's value from the
catalogue's. Added a notice for output above the configured window, since that
clamp was silent too.

Pin the four gpt-5-chat-latest windows in token_limit_overrides: the
modelTotalTokens merge path overwrites unconditionally, and a source reporting
no context window for these could let the wrong value back in and recreate
output == total on a gated profile.

The gate's exit 1 aborted the scheduled job before the keyless sync and the
Create Pull Request step, so one stale profile would have halted model updates
for all 12 providers every week with nobody paged. The sync steps now continue
on error, the PR is created either way with the gate findings rendered into its
body, and a final step fails the run so it stays visibly red.

Overrides no longer count as confirmed limits under --no-config-overrides,
where they are not applied to the catalogue either.

* fix(llm): decide the rejection warning on the value that is actually sent

The check read the configured value, but validate_max_tokens caps it before the
request goes out: 128,000 configured under a 16,384 window is sent as 16,384,
which the provider accepts. Saying it would be rejected was wrong in exactly
the case where the cap saves the call.

Compare the effective value - min(output, total, MAX_OUTPUT_TOKENS) - against
the model's limit, and report the cap itself separately, since that is silent
too and reads at run time as the model refusing to write more.

* fix(config): name a config key that is almost, but not quite, a real one

A key the engine does not recognise is copied into the merged config and never
read again, so the node runs with a default the author believes they overrode.
Nothing warns at publish time or at run time; the pipeline reads as correct.

The distance between the typo and the symptom is what makes it expensive:

services.json never declares (score, similarity, renderChunkSize, table), and
flagging those on every run would teach people to ignore the message. So the
check reports only a near-certain miss - a known key that ends with the
unknown one, which is the dropped-prefix mistake, or a difflib match at 0.9.

* fix(text-output): install smbprotocol at module level and fix anonymize crash

- Move depends() to module level in endpoint.py so smbprotocol is always
  installed regardless of OPEN_MODE.
- Fix STATUS_HEAP_CORRUPTION in anonymize by removing the ThreadPoolExecutor
  from glinerRecognizer.predict(); GLiNER/PyTorch is not thread-safe and
  concurrent calls on the same model corrupt the native heap.

Fixes #1165

* Remove 'name' property from text output services

* fix(text-output): define the SMB fields the parameters object references

The build validated services.json and rejected it:

  Exit: InvalidName (ap:0x27) services.cpp:428
  Field name smb.storePath was not found in .../text_output/services.json

text_output.target.parameters listed smb.storePath, smb.server,
smb.username and smb.password, but no field by those names exists in the
node or in nodes/src/nodes/core. The engine resolves every referenced
property against a definition, so the node failed to load and the build
died on all three platforms.

storePath is already a core field, so it is referenced bare, matching
local_text_output. server, username and password have no core definition,
so they are defined locally under the node namespace, matching the
store_astra pattern where astra_db.api_endpoint reaches the node as
api_endpoint. That lines the shape up with what endpoint.py already
reads: parameters.get('server'), get('username'), get('password') and
get('storePath').

The password field is marked secure with a password widget and the
127-character limit that validateConfig already enforces.

* fix(text-output): fail validation on SMB config errors, keep reachability advisory

The connect() probe this PR enabled reported every failure as a warning, so a
rejected credential or a wrong share name passed validateConfig.

Split the two cases instead:

- EACCES, EPERM and ENOENT fail validation. Each is a configuration mistake
  the user has to fix. connect() already tolerates ENOENT on the store path
  (it is created on first write), so an ENOENT arriving here came from the
  share root and means the share name is wrong.
- Everything else stays a warning. Validation also runs on the Platform host,
  which often has no route to the customer's share, and rejecting a correct
  configuration there was the reason the probe had been commented out.

Also document both lifecycle no-ops in IGlobal, and correct the README, which
still claimed the connection was not tested during configuration validation.

* fix(text-output): classify SMB failures by NtStatus, scope credentials, keep GLiNER parallel

The errno-based split shipped in the previous commit did not work. Verified
against smbprotocol 1.17.0:

- SMBAuthenticationError derives from SMBException, not OSError, so a rejected
  credential carried no errno and was downgraded to a warning. That is the one
  case the README called a blocking configuration mistake.
- STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED is absent from SMBOSError's errno table, so it arrives
  with errno 0 and the EACCES branch never fired either.
- errno EPERM comes from STATUS_SHARING_VIOLATION ("file in use by another
  process"), which is transient, so treating it as a config error was wrong.

Classify on NtStatus instead, with an explicit SMBAuthenticationError branch.
Rejected, wrong or expired credentials, access denied, privilege not held, a
missing share (STATUS_BAD_NETWORK_NAME) and missing names or paths now fail
validation. Timeouts, dropped transports, refused connections and sharing
violations warn without rejecting.

Also:

- Register credentials with register_session() against the configured server
  instead of the process-wide ClientConfig singleton. Validation runs this now,
  so one endpoint could otherwise overwrite the credential another endpoint was
  already connected with.
- Restore the GLiNER thread pool and hold a lock around predict_entities only.
  Removing the pool fixed the crash but serialized chunking, offset arithmetic
  and overlap filtering with it. Output is unchanged: results are sorted and
  deduplicated before returning, verified identical to the sequential version
  across multi-chunk, overlap-boundary and dense-entity inputs.
- Correct the README, which described the old global credential registration.

Tests: 25 for validateConfig covering both failure classes, the smbprotocol
hierarchy facts the classification depends on, and probe scope; 11 for
predict() covering absolute offsets, overlap dedup, single-chunk input,
determinism across runs, forward-pass serialization and label batching.

… them (#2162)

* fix(nodes): deprecate claude-opus-4-1, retired by Anthropic

Anthropic retired claude-opus-4-1-20250805 on 2026-08-05 and the API now
answers not_found_error. The profile is still offered, so anyone selecting it
gets failing requests that never reach the usage page.

The model sync cannot reach this on its own: the profile carries
modelSource: openrouter, so _source_is_authoritative() lets only OpenRouter
deprecate it, and OpenRouter still lists anthropic/claude-opus-4.1 with no
expiration date. Marked by hand until that gap is closed.

* fix(sync_models): a hand-marked deprecation is no longer undone by the sync

_source_is_authoritative received two vocabularies and recognised neither
fully: the deprecation path passes display labels ('Anthropic API'), the
enrichment path passes internal keys ('openrouter'), and the function compared
against 'provider API' and 'OpenRouter'. So the native API could never
deprecate a profile, and OpenRouter could never lift one - the reverse of what
the docstring describes. Normalise both vocabularies to one key.

That fix alone would delete the deprecation added in this branch on the next
run, since OpenRouter still lists claude-opus-4.1. So record deprecatedBy when
the sync marks a profile, and only lift a mark the sync itself made. A profile
deprecated by hand carries no deprecatedBy and stays: a provider that keeps
listing a model it has retired is precisely why someone marks one by hand, so
seeing it in the listing again is not evidence to the contrary.

Without this the four hand-marked gemini profiles would be reinstated on the
next sync with a Gemini key, since models.list() still returns retired models.

* fix(sync_models): decide deprecation authority on canonical source keys

Review feedback on the ownership model.

The lift required deprecatedBy to name the same source that is running, but the
OpenRouter expiration branch stamps a mark without checking authority and can
therefore mark a 'provider' profile. Matching on the stamp left that profile
deprecated with no source able to clear it - worse than the behaviour it
replaced. Any source with authority over the profile may now lift a mark the
sync applied; hand-applied marks carry no deprecatedBy and stay protected
either way.

Authority is decided on canonical keys ('provider'/'openrouter'/'litellm')
threaded from primary_source, replacing the label heuristic that would have
granted provider authority to any future '<Something> API' string. The display
label stays prose for the migration message.

A mark left standing while the source lists the model again is now reported
instead of landing in unchanged, which surfaces the existing hand-marked
profiles that need a one-time decision.

* fix(sync_models): a standing deprecation mark is not a pure skip

has_changes() drove an early return that rendered a provider as SKIPPED and
moved on, so a provider whose only finding was a profile listed again while
still deprecated had that finding dropped from both the console output and the
PR body - the exact case the previous commit added the report line for.

* feat(sync_models): re-verify catalogue models by calling them

The smoke gate validates additions only: a model already in services.json is
accepted without being called, so one that entered correctly and was retired
six months later stays in the catalogue forever. The live test does not catch
it either - it asks the listing endpoint, and providers keep returning models
they have retired, with generateContent among the supported methods, refusing
only when the model is actually called.

--verify-existing calls every active profile and deprecates the ones the
provider reports as gone, carrying over the replacement the provider names when
it names one. Only a message identifying the model as unavailable qualifies; a
rate limit or a permission error never deprecates anything.

That evidence bypasses the authority rule, deliberately. Absence from a listing
means little across sources - an OpenRouter alias missing from a provider's API
is expected - but a direct refusal does not: a profile discovered through
OpenRouter is just as unusable once the provider behind it has retired the
model, and OpenRouter will keep listing it regardless.

The gemini live test now makes one real call per profile instead of trusting
the listing, which is the check it always claimed to be.

* fix(nodes): deprecate the five gemini profiles the API refuses to run

Verified with a real generateContent call per profile against a current key,
which is what --verify-existing does: models/gemini-2.5-pro, 2.5-flash,
2.5-flash-lite, 2.5-pro-preview and 2.5-pro-preview-05-06 all answer 404,
'no longer available to new users'. All five are still listed by models.list()
with generateContent among their supported methods, which is why nothing had
noticed.

Google names the replacement for three of them and those go into the migration
notes; the two preview IDs are simply gone with nothing suggested.

Also repointed two existing notes: gemini-2.0-flash and 2.0-flash-lite were
directing people to 2.5-flash and 2.5-flash-lite, both of which are in this
same batch. Every migration target now resolves to a profile that runs.

* fix(sync_models): classify a failed call, and keep call-made marks out of the listing path

Two problems the larger scope introduced.

A call-verified retirement was stamped deprecatedBy: 'provider', which the lift
path reads as ordinary listing evidence. The premise of the feature is that the
provider still lists the model, so the next scheduled run - which never passes
--verify-existing - would find it listed, find the provider authoritative, and
resurrect it, deleting the replacement note. With the flag on every run it would
churn every other run. Such a mark now records 'provider-call', deliberately
outside SOURCE_KEYS so the listing path cannot touch it, and is lifted only by a
call that passes.

Retirement was decided by substring matching a flattened string, and the guard
meant to keep transient errors out never ran, because base.py passed reason (a
str) where an Exception was expected. Worse, the patterns matched access-gated
404s: OpenAI answers 'does not exist or you do not have access to it' for a
retired model and for one the key cannot reach, and Anthropic returns
not_found_error for org-restricted models, so a CI key without a tier would have
deprecated every gated-but-live model in one run.

Classification moves to the smoke layer and reads the typed exception. A bare
404 is now 'missing' - reported, never acted on - and only a provider stating
the model is gone yields 'retired'. Verified against the live Gemini API: the
three models Google declares retired classify as retired, the two ambiguous 404s
as missing, a live model passes.

* fix(sync_models): an OpenRouter expiry only deprecates what OpenRouter owns

The expiration branch changed deprecation state with no authority check, so an
entry OpenRouter marks expired could deprecate a 'provider' or 'manual' profile
whose model the native API still serves - and a keyless run is enough to do it.

This is the smallest of the two fixes offered in review; the other one (letting
an authoritative source lift any sync-applied mark) is already in. Both belong:
one stops the wrong profile being marked, the other stops a mark being stranded.
Ownership now reads the same in every direction - absence, expiry and lifting -
while a direct call still overrides it, since a model that will not run is gone
whoever discovered it.

* fix(sync_models): a majority of retirements is an API failure, not a catalogue dying

Review feedback, and the loose end in the verification: a retirement message is
per-model evidence, but a break one level up produces the same message for every
model at once. Retire an API version and every call answers with the same 404
carrying the same wording - which is exactly what the retirement phrases match -
and a single run would deprecate the whole provider.

Above half the verified models, the run now deprecates nothing, moves those
findings to the unverified list and warns. Providers do not retire most of a
catalogue at once, so a majority verdict says more about the API than about the
models; a real mass retirement is then applied deliberately rather than swept in.

The threshold check is a named function so the boundary is pinned by tests
rather than inferred from a run: five of twenty-six is believed, exactly half is
not a majority, and a verified count of zero is never judged.

* feat(tool_notion): add Notion tool node

Exposes a Notion workspace (search, pages, databases) to agents as
eight tools, targeting the 2025-09-03 database/data-source API split
(Notion-Version 2026-03-11) rather than the older single-database
shape. No live workspace has exercised this end-to-end, so the node
is marked experimental.

* fix(tool_notion): address CodeRabbit findings on parent type, title property, trash field, and write retries

Verified each finding directly against developers.notion.com before
applying:

- parent.type must be "page_id"/"data_source_id", not the bare
  "page"/"data_source" the create-page body was sending.
- A data source's title property isn't always called "Name" (e.g.
  "Task") -- look it up from the schema instead of guessing.
- The update-page and get-page paths used a nonexistent "archived"
  field; the real fields are "in_trash" (request) and "in_trash"/
  "is_archived" (response).
- Writes (create/update/append) no longer retry: Notion has no
  idempotency key for these endpoints, so retrying a mutation whose
  response was lost to a connection error risked creating duplicate
  pages or content.
- notion_append_content now batches into groups of <=100 blocks and
  rejects lines over 2000 characters, matching Notion's documented
  request limits.
- Pin requests>=2.34.2 as a baseline floor.

Declined: collapsing credentials.json's two apikey catalog entries
into one. Verified via credentials.py that this does make both
entries required for "configured" status, but the same generator
output (a prefix-keyed path plus a node-name-keyed path, both
required) already exists uncurated on every other tool_* node with a
single apikey field (tool_apify, tool_exa_search, tool_deepl,
tool_tavily) -- a pre-existing, repo-wide generator behavior, not a
defect introduced by this node.

* fix(tool_notion): drop the nonexistent is_archived fallback in notion_get_page

Re-verified against Notion's page object reference and changelog:
"archived" was deprecated in April 2024 and fully removed/renamed to
"in_trash" in API version 2026-03-11 -- they are the same state under
old/new names, not two independent fields. The "is_archived" name
came from an earlier, less authoritative fetch and doesn't actually
exist on the current page object; reading it was harmless (always
None) but implied a real field that isn't there.

* docs(tool_notion): add shared-surface entries for the Notion node

Adds the three shared-surface pieces flagged in review: the node
catalog row in docs/README-nodes.md, the CHANGELOG entry, and the
generated params block in the node's README.

* feat(tool_crustdata): add Crustdata company/people search as an agent tool

Adds tool_crustdata, giving an agent B2B discovery: company_search and
person_search against Crustdata's filter-based /company/search and
/person-docs/search API. Same pattern as tool_exa_search (single API
key, plain requests, no vendor SDK, structured {success, ...} JSON
returns, no pipeline lanes).

UNVERIFIED SURFACE (#2129): built from Crustdata's public docs, not
against a live account. The filters shape (list of {filter_type, type,
value}) and both endpoints are corroborated across multiple doc pages,
but the exhaustive filter_type enum and exact response envelope
aren't confirmed -- response parsing is deliberately defensive
(_extract_records tries several plausible top-level keys) rather than
assuming one exact shape. Marked experimental for the same reason.

Also registers the node's mock apikey in the dynamic test framework's
per-node credential table (nodes/test/framework/pipeline.py), matching
every other apikey-gated tool node -- without it the framework's own
pipeline-open test fails on the empty placeholder key that ships in
the real default profile.

* fix(tool_crustdata): correct the search contract per Crustdata's real API reference

CodeRabbit's review on #2130 flagged that the endpoint/filter shape
this node shipped with didn't match Crustdata's current API. Verified
independently by fetching docs.crustdata.com's own versioned reference
pages directly (not paraphrased) -- three prior research passes (mine,
CodeRabbit's, and a third-party dev's notes) had disagreed with each
other, so this reads the primary source rather than trusting any one
of them:

- person_search now hits /person/search, not /person-docs/search.
- filters are now a list of {field, type, value} conditions the node
  wraps into Crustdata's {op, conditions} group form, not a bare array
  of {filter_type, type, value} sent as-is.
- pagination is now cursor-based (cursor in, next_cursor/total_count
  out), not the page integer the node sent before -- Crustdata's API
  doesn't have a page parameter at all.
- limit range widened to the documented 1-1000 (was 1-100, an
  invented number).
- added an optional sorts passthrough, since Crustdata's docs warn a
  missing/changed sort order invalidates the pagination cursor.

Also, from CodeRabbit's other two findings:
- IGlobal.beginGlobal() no longer raises out of the engine lifecycle
  on a malformed defaultLimit (e.g. an empty string from a hand-edited
  .pipe file bypassing the UI's own type coercion) -- extracted
  _coerce_limit(), used by both beginGlobal and a new validateConfig
  warning, with tests for the malformed-input paths.
- test_timeout_is_reported_as_a_structured_error_not_raised now mocks
  time.sleep like the other retry tests; it was previously the one
  test in the suite that actually slept out its ~14s of backoff.

The module docstring, README, and services.json capability comment
are updated from "unverified surface" to "verified against Crustdata's
reference, not yet against a live account" -- the schema is no longer
a guess, only the untested runtime behavior (plan-tier gating, the
full per-entity field enum) remains open per #2129.

* fix(tool_crustdata): drop all_of from the generic match parameter

CodeRabbit's second review pass on #2130 flagged that 'match' offered
'all_of' as a third option alongside 'and'/'or'. Verified independently
against the actual OpenAPI schema for the company search endpoint
(docs.crustdata.com/api-reference/company-apis/search-companies-with-
indexed-fields-only): its op enum is exactly ['and', 'or'] -- all_of
isn't a company-search option at all.

Person search does document all_of, but it isn't a generic combinator:
it's constrained to a single nested-array field path (employment,
education, ...), rejects scalar fields, can't hold negation operators,
and can't nest another all_of/has_all inside it. None of that fits a
flat "combine any conditions" match parameter shared by both tools, so
it's dropped from the schema entirely rather than exposed and silently
misbehaving on the conditions an agent actually sends.

* fix(tool_crustdata): use shared post_with_retry, coerce per-call limit

Addresses joshuadarron's review on #2130: the hand-rolled retry loop
dropped ConnectionError retries (the same regression tool_tavily shipped
and fixed); switching to the shared post_with_retry helper fixes that and
matches the tool_tavily/tool_v0/tool_deepl convention. Also reuses
_coerce_limit for the per-call "limit" argument so a stringy value like
"50" from the model isn't silently discarded, and adds tool_crustdata to
the docs/README-nodes.md catalog.

* fix(tool_crustdata): patch tenacity.nap.time.sleep, not nap.sleep

CodeRabbit caught it on #2130: tenacity's BaseRetrying binds its sleep
default at import time (sleep: Callable = sleep), so patching the
tenacity.nap.sleep attribute afterward doesn't touch the callable
Retrying actually invokes. It still calls time.sleep under the hood, so
that's the real patch target. Confirmed empirically — the previous target
let real sleeps run (test file took ~44s), the fix drops it to ~0.3s
with identical assertions passing.

* fix(tool_google_workspace): make check_connection actually probe the API

connection_ok was derived only from local checks (client constructed,
token scopes claimed) for gmail/drive/docs/sheets, since check_connection
called _check_connection_impl() without a probe. calendar was the only
service with a live probe wired, so a disabled Google API on the caller's
project was invisible everywhere else — connection_ok: true while every
real call 403'd.

- Wire a live probe for gmail (users().getProfile), drive (about().get),
  and docs/sheets (a made-up-id get(), swallowing the expected 404 since
  neither API has a list/about endpoint to probe cheaply).
- _check_connection_impl no longer defaults to True when no probe runs;
  it reports 'unknown' instead, and fixes a bug where the scope-coverage
  check could silently coerce that sentinel back to a bool.
- execute() now attaches the structured Google reason code (e.g.
  accessNotConfigured vs forbidden vs rateLimitExceeded) to raised
  errors, surfaced as errorReason.

Closes #1694

* test,docs(tool_google_workspace): decouple test fixtures, fix scope-check wording

Test fixtures for the accessNotConfigured probe-failure case set _HttpErr's
raw HTTP reason to the same string as the structured JSON body's error
reason ('accessNotConfigured' both places). errorReason is verified to come
exclusively from the parsed JSON body (_error_reason_code never reads
.reason), but with both fields equal, the test couldn't tell that apart from
a future regression that accidentally read the generic .reason instead.
Decoupled all four (docs/drive/gmail/sheets): .reason is now 'Forbidden',
'accessNotConfigured' stays only in the JSON payload. Verified by temporarily
making _error_reason_code read exc.reason directly -- all four then fail
with 'Forbidden' != 'accessNotConfigured' as expected, confirming they'd
catch that exact regression; reverted and confirmed the real implementation
passes all four again.

README diagnostics bullets (docs/drive/gmail/sheets) said check_connection
"verifies that granted OAuth scopes cover the configured access tier and
probes the API" as one combined behavior. _check_connection_impl runs the
live probe unconditionally regardless of auth type, but only runs
token_scope_report inside `if auth_type == 'user':` -- service-account
connections get probed but never get a scope check (there's no per-user
grant to check). Reworded to state the two facts separately with their
actual conditions.

* fix(tool_google_workspace): parse the One Platform error shape, fix calendar docs drift

_error_reason_code only read the legacy error.errors[] body (Gmail,
Drive). Sheets and Docs are One Platform APIs and carry the reason
in error.details[] as a google.rpc.ErrorInfo instead, with no
errors[] array at all -- so a disabled Sheets/Docs API, the actual
#1694 scenario, never got an errorReason. Now parses both shapes,
falling back further to the coarser error.status when even
ErrorInfo is absent. _is_rate_limit_403 normalizes the
SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE ErrorInfo reasons to match its existing set.

Also:
- calendar's tool description and README now use the same "live
  probe + scope coverage" wording already applied to the other four
  services.
- raise the probe-error truncation cap (200 -> 500 chars) so the
  actionable guidance clause isn't cut mid-sentence.
- a scope-check failure no longer overwrites a probe failure's
  error message; it now reports separately as scopeError (with the
  two tests that asserted the old key updated to match).

* fix(llm): send adaptive thinking shape to Claude 5 models

Claude 4.7+ (including the whole Claude 5 family) rejects
thinking={'type': 'enabled', 'budget_tokens': N} with HTTP 400; only
{'type': 'adaptive'} is accepted. The gate in
build_anthropic_thinking_kwargs only routed claude-opus-4-7/4-8 to the
adaptive shape, so every Claude 5 profile in the llm_anthropic enum
(claude-sonnet-5, claude-fable-5, claude-opus-5, and the -latest
aliases) passed validate() but failed at runtime on the first LLM call.

Invert the gate into an explicit legacy allowlist (Claude 3.x, 4.0,
4.1, 4.5 incl. Haiku 4.5, 4.6, Mythos Preview): unknown and future
model names now default to the current adaptive shape instead of the
removed one, so a new enum entry can no longer silently inherit the
rejected shape. Behavior for every previously-working model is
unchanged, including the Claude 3/3.5 Haiku exclusion and the legacy
budget arithmetic.

The new test suite pins the shape per model family, and a group test
parses the node's services.json profile enum and fails if any enum
model lacks a declared expected shape — so adding a profile forces an
explicit thinking-shape decision.

Fixes #1911

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(llm): match legacy thinking ids by whole segment, keep haiku-latest legacy

Addresses both review findings on #1917.

1. claude-haiku-latest regressed to the adaptive shape. The alias resolves
   to Haiku 4.5, which only accepts {'type': 'enabled', 'budget_tokens': N},
   and the profile carries extendedThinking so the builder runs for it.
   Before the PR it fell through to the legacy shape and worked; the new
   allowlist missed it, reintroducing the #1911 failure mode on a
   previously-working profile. The test map declared it 'adaptive', so it
   asserted the regression instead of catching it. Add the alias to the
   legacy set, flip its expected shape, and name it in the README row.

2. Legacy matching used open-ended prefixes, so a future claude-sonnet-4-50
   matched claude-sonnet-4-5 and claude-opus-4-20 matched claude-opus-4-2
   (a prefix that only existed to catch dated ids), handing unknown models
   the removed shape. Match whole ids instead, after stripping -YYYYMMDD
   dated and -fast deployment suffixes, so dated ids still resolve to their
   base model while longer version numbers do not inherit a shorter one.
   The claude-3- family rule keeps its trailing hyphen, which is already a
   whole-segment match.

Adds regression cases for claude-sonnet-4-50 / claude-opus-4-20 / claude-30-*
and direct coverage of the suffix-stripping helper. Verified by mutating each
defect back in individually: the haiku change fails 2 tests, the prefix change
fails 6, and all 98 pass with both fixed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(llm): normalize composed model-id suffixes in either order

Addresses the second round of review findings on #1917.

1. (Major) _anthropic_base_model_id stripped the dated suffix once, then a
   deployment suffix once, so the two only composed in one order. An id like
   claude-opus-4-6-20251101-fast ends in -fast, so the -YYYYMMDD regex did
   not match; stripping -fast then left claude-opus-4-6-20251101, which
   misses the legacy allowlist and takes the adaptive shape a 4.6 model
   rejects. Strip repeatedly until the id stops changing, so both orders
   reduce to the same base. Each pass strictly shortens the id, so the loop
   terminates.

   hardening rather than a live break — but it is the same failure class the
   helper exists to prevent.

2. (Minor) The README legacy row claimed all of Claude 3.x while the row
   above it exempts Claude 3 / 3.5 Haiku from thinking entirely. Scope the
   legacy row to Claude 3.x except those two.

enabled) and Claude 5 ids (must stay adaptive, so normalization cannot drag
a new model into the legacy shape). Verified by restoring single-pass
normalization: 4 tests fail, and all 106 pass with the loop.

…ce (#2165)

* fix(task): tell the caller when useExisting returned a running instance

use() with useExisting accepts a pipeline, ignores it when a task with that
token is already running, and returns the live instance with a response
identical to a fresh launch. The caller has no way to tell that the
configuration it just sent was not applied.

An A/B comparison across two pipeline versions returns the same numbers for
both and reads as 'the change had no effect'. A configuration error that was
already fixed keeps reappearing, because the value lives on in an instance the
file no longer describes. The instance also carries whatever state earlier runs
left behind, so a benchmark's later runs benefit from its earlier ones.

Add 'reused' to the response, and say in the log when the submitted pipeline
differs from the running one. Reuse stays the default - it is what keeps a warm
instance cheap; what was missing is that it was invisible.

* fix(task): a restart updates the pipeline the control describes

restart_task swapped the running configuration but left control.pipeline
holding whatever was launched first, which the docstring already said it
should update. The comparison added in this PR then read a record of something
that is no longer running: restart(P2) followed by use(P2, useExisting) - the
documented way to apply new configuration to a live token - warned that the
submitted pipeline differed, while resubmitting the replaced one passed
silently. Exactly backwards.

* fix(task): store a restarted pipeline in the shape a launch would

A launch stamps the resolved source onto the pipeline and gives the source
component an empty config when it has none. restart_task stored the raw
request, so the same pipeline submitted again arrived normalised and compared
unequal to what was stored - the comparison reporting a difference that the
launch itself had introduced.

Both paths now go through one helper, so they cannot drift apart again.

* fix(task): validate the restarted pipeline before the task is stopped

_apply_source_defaults raises when the source component is missing, so calling
it after restart_task made it a validation that runs too late: the task is
already stopped, Task.restart_task already holds the new pipeline, and
control.pipeline still names the old one - three views of the world and none of
them running.

Normalising first also removes the second call: the same object goes to
restart_task and to the control, so they cannot describe different things.

* fix(task): refuse a restart that names a different source

The source is part of the task's identity and a restart cannot change it, as
restart_task's own docstring says. But _apply_source_defaults stamps the
control's source onto the pipeline, so a request naming a different one was
overwritten without a word: the caller would believe it had switched source and
be told nothing.

Compared before the helper runs, so the request is refused rather than quietly
rewritten.

… (#1823)

* fix(ai): name the cause when a reasoning model is cut off mid-<think>

The strip regex needs a closing </think>, so a model that exhausts its
output budget while still reasoning reaches json.loads with the block
intact and fails at character zero:

    JSONDecodeError: Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0)

That is indistinguishable from a bad schema, malformed JSON, or a model
returning prose -- all of which have different fixes. This one is
modelOutputTokens (chat.py:100, default 4096), and nothing said so. It is
also intermittent by nature, since whether reasoning fits in budget
depends on the input, which pushes people toward blaming the data.

Checked after the substitution rather than before, so a complete block
followed by a truncated one is caught too.

Refs #1822

* fix(ai): fail fast on a truncated <think> block instead of retrying it

The previous commit named the cause but nothing carried it: the only
production caller, ChatBase.chat's expectJson loop, catches
(json.JSONDecodeError, ValueError). So the new message was swallowed, two
more model calls went out asking the model to "examine your JSON and ensure
it is complete" -- an instruction that describes a problem that does not
exist -- and the caller finally got the generic "Failed to get valid JSON
response after N attempts", which names nothing.

parseJson now raises ThinkTruncatedError, a ValueError subclass declared next
to it, so chat.py can branch on the type rather than match the message.
chat.py lists that arm before the generic one and re-raises immediately: a
resample rarely fits a budget that has already overflowed, and each attempt
is a paid call. What escapes reaches the user intact -- LLMBase.writeQuestions
renders it as "**LLM error** - ThinkTruncatedError: model was cut off inside
a <think> block ...".

The generic arm now carries its cause too (`Cause: {e}` and `from e`). The
underlying parse error was being dropped entirely, leaving the caller a
truncated response and no statement of what was wrong with it.

Both clauses of the guard are kept, and a test pins why. re.sub is a single
left-to-right pass, so deleting an inner pair can splice a fresh one into
text the pass has already moved past: '<thi<think>x</think>nk>a</think>{...}'
leaves '<think>a</think>{...}', which opens with <think> and is not a
truncation. Without the closing-tag test that would be misreported as a
budget problem.

Adds test_chat_expect_json_retries.py -- nothing drove ChatBase.chat before,
so the retry loop was untested. Five of its assertions fail on the previous
head: fail-fast, the surviving message, the carried cause, the class of the
final error, and that the repair prompt is never sent.

Refs #1822

* test(ai): cover a truncation found on a retry, and tidy the new suite

Self-review of the previous commit found one real coverage gap and four
consistency nits, all in the new test file. No production code changes.

The gap: the fail-fast arm sits inside the loop, so it holds on attempt 2 and
3 as well as attempt 1, and nothing pinned that. It is also the likelier
production shape -- the first answer is merely malformed, the repair prompt
makes the model reason harder about getting the JSON right, and that is what
pushes it over the output budget. Six assertions now fail on 74236074,
up from five.

The nits: moved the "not reported as exhausted retries" case out of
TestOrdinaryBadJson, where it was misfiled, into TestTruncatedThinkBlock;
switched typing.List to the builtin generics the neighbouring chat tests use;
lifted the fixture strings to module constants so the repair-prompt marker is
stated once; and tightened the __cause__ assertion from "is not None" to the
JSONDecodeError it should actually be.

Refs #1822

* fix(ai): do not blame modelOutputTokens when the JSON did arrive

A missing </think> is not by itself proof of a budget overflow. A model can
finish reasoning, emit its JSON, and simply drop the closing tag -- which is
what happens when the tag is consumed as a stop sequence. Review of #1823 found
'<think>reasoning\n{"a": 1}' taking the truncation path, where the response is
still unparseable but modelOutputTokens is not the fix, so the diagnosis sends
the operator to a setting that cannot help and the fail-fast arm also spends the
repair retries that might have recovered it.

Require the remainder to hold no object or array opener before claiming the
model never reached the JSON. When one is present this falls through to the
ordinary parse error, which is what such input got before the check existed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01XhknhdhTcbEPP6LeXSdFF8

* fix(ai): decode the tail instead of looking for a brace

The previous commit skipped the truncation diagnosis whenever '{' or '[' appeared
after an unclosed <think>. That character is a poor proxy: a model reasoning its
way toward JSON writes one constantly -- "the schema is {title, body}" is an
ordinary sentence in that chain -- so the test waved through most genuine
truncations, which is precisely the case #1822 reports.

Ask whether a complete JSON value can actually be decoded. _holdsCompleteJson
walks each opener and tries raw_decode there, so '{title, body}' and
'compare [A, B]' are correctly still truncations, while '<think>reasoning
{"a": 1}' -- a real response whose closing tag was consumed as a stop sequence --
still falls through to the ordinary parse error.

Reasoning that quotes valid JSON inline before being cut off remains unflagged;
that is the behaviour this check has always had and narrowing it further would
need position tracking for no realistic gain.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01XhknhdhTcbEPP6LeXSdFF8

* fix(ai): require the decoded JSON to run to the end

_holdsCompleteJson discarded raw_decode's end position, so a JSON value decoded
ANYWHERE counted. That misses the likeliest truncation of all: a model drafting
its answer mid-reasoning and being cut off after it -- '<think>I will return
{"title": "X"} and then add the' leaves a fragment that decodes perfectly and is
still followed by prose. Keep the end position and require the value to reach the
end of the string, allowing trailing whitespace and a closing fence.

Only objects and arrays count as starts. parseJson does accept a bare scalar, but
no model answers an expectJson prompt with one, whereas reasoning that breaks off
on a number or on the word "true" is an ordinary truncation -- honouring scalars
would trade a real case for an imaginary one. Both shapes are pinned as tests so
the choice is enforced rather than asserted.

Adds regressions for an embedded JSON fragment and for a draft followed by prose.
